Try Materials.Ai David Willson 07.31.2026 MRO Time to read: 10 min Industrial equipment is built for longevity, but the components that keep it running are not always built to last. Many production systems operate reliably for 20–30 years, while the mechanical parts, control systems, and electronic components they depend on can become difficult or impossible to source before the equipment wears out. The gap between a machine’s operating life and the lifecycle of its critical parts is the “MRO obsolescence mismatch”—a foreseeable problem that grows gradually rather than hitting all at once. Why Parts Age Faster Than Equipment When OEMs update product lines to improve performance or follow new standards, older components are often phased out while the equipment they support still has years of productive life remaining. This is a normal lifecycle dynamic for different types of components operating on different schedules, and availability doesn’t always track with equipment longevity. For control and electronic components , this shift often begins with a formal signal: an end-of-life (EOL) notice for a specific PLC module , sensor, drive, or switch that moves parts into last-time-buy status before they disappear from normal distribution channels entirely. For mechanical parts—gearboxes, seals, bearings, hydraulic manifolds, or structural castings—availability declines more quietly. A supplier discontinues a casting run, a proprietary geometry disappears from catalogs, or minimum order quantities become uneconomical for a single facility. There is often no formal notice at all. In both cases, sourcing shifts from routine procurement to locating remaining inventory, qualifying compatible alternatives, or evaluating repair and fabrication options—ideally before a critical failure forces the issue. Learn how to build a long-term strategy for aging assets with Fictiv’s MRO solutions for obsolete and hard-to-source parts. The Four-Stage Obsolescence Timeline Understanding where equipment sits in this lifecycle allows maintenance, engineering, and procurement teams to anticipate sourcing challenges rather than react to them. The following four stages illustrate how MRO parts obsolescence evolves over time and the actions that can reduce risk before a critical failure disrupts production . Equipment Age Operational State Primary Risk Recommended Action Years 1-5 Equipment fully supported Complacency Document BOMs, classify critical spares, capture design data, and monitor early EOL notices. Years 6-10 OEM support begins shrinking Early sourcing gaps Monitor EOL notices, track supplier catalog, identify points of failure, and evaluate alternatives Years 11-20 Reactive maintenance becomes common Unsupported parts and long lead times Use reverse engineering, custom fabrication, and on-demand manufacturing, while evaluating long-term replacement options. Years 21-30 OEM support is largely gone Production uptime depends on independent sourcing Maintain a long-term supply strategy, pre-manufacture critical spares, maintain strategic inventory, and evaluate equipment replacement. Years 1-5: Full Throughput and OEM Support During the first five years, OEM support is fully available, and standard replacement parts are readily accessible through normal supply channels. This is the lowest-risk phase of the equipment lifecycle. The asset is operating as designed, and replacement parts can typically be sourced through authorized distributors with predictable lead times. The primary risk during this stage is complacency. Because parts are easy to obtain, organizations often delay updating BOMs, identifying critical spare parts, or capturing engineering documentation . These gaps may not affect current operations, but can significantly complicate sourcing as OEM support changes over time. Use this period to build the foundation for long-term equipment support. Document complete BOMs , classify critical spare parts, identify points of failure, and capture technical documentation while it is readily available. Where appropriate, establish baseline CAD models or dimensional records for components that may eventually require reverse engineering. Years 6-10: Early Obsolescence and the First Sourcing Gaps Between years six and ten, OEM product redesigns begin creating the first gaps in part availability. OEMs begin refreshing product lines, retiring older components, and issuing EOL notices for selected parts. While replacement parts remain available, inventories become less predictable, lead times increase, and sourcing requires greater coordination. The risk shifts from underlying equipment reliability to part availability. Critical components such as bearings, seals, gearboxes, or hydraulic manifolds may become difficult to source, and compatible replacements may require engineering validation. Delaying action until a component fails reduces sourcing options and increases the likelihood of production delays. Monitor supplier EOL notices, review BOMs for components approaching end of support, and identify single points of failure. Evaluate approved alternative or cross-referenced parts before inventories tighten further, and reassess inventory strategies and policies for components with declining availability. Years 11-20: Reactive Maintenance and Unsupported Parts From years eleven through twenty, unsupported parts increasingly require manual sourcing, custom fabrication, or reverse engineering to keep equipment operational. Although many production assets continue to operate reliably, OEM support has diminished for critical components. Standard procurement channels no longer guarantee replacement parts, forcing maintenance teams to search surplus inventories, specialty suppliers, or third-party repair providers. Part sourcing becomes increasingly reactive. Every unexpected failure has the potential to trigger emergency sourcing, engineering reviews, or custom manufacturing while production remains idle. For mechanical components, failure modes often announce themselves through vibration, noise, or a gradual drop in performance—but by that stage, replacement parts may no longer be readily available. Shift from reactive sourcing to proactive lifecycle planning. Identify critical components for reverse engineering before they fail using technologies such as 3D scanning, CMM measurement, and CAD remodeling when original drawings are unavailable. Combine these capabilities with on-demand CNC machining and additive manufacturing to reduce dependence on obsolete OEM supply chains and extend the service life of legacy equipment. Years 21-30: Uptime Seriously at Risk After two decades of service, reverse engineering and on-demand manufacturing become essential because OEM support for many critical parts has effectively ended. The equipment may still provide significant production value, but maintaining uptime increasingly depends on an organization’s ability to source or manufacture replacement parts independently. The greatest risk is extended production downtime caused by the inability to replace a failed component quickly. Emergency hot-shipping, incomplete documentation, and last-minute engineering workarounds become increasingly common when no long-term sourcing strategy is in place. Develop an independent supply strategy for the asset’s remaining useful life. Identify critical wear components for pre-fabrication, maintain strategic spare part inventories based on failure history and remaining part life, and partner with qualified manufacturers capable of reverse engineering and producing obsolete components on demand. Examples of MRO spare parts The Real Costs of Parts Life Mismatch When critical components fail and OEM support is no longer available, maintenance teams face limited options. Remaining inventory may need to be sourced through secondary suppliers. It may be necessary to qualify an alternative component, commission a custom-fabricated replacement, or reverse engineer the original part, all while production remains halted. If technical drawings, specifications, or BOMs are incomplete, additional time is spent measuring parts, validating dimensions, or recreating design intent before manufacturing can begin. These documentation gaps compound delays, particularly for legacy assets that have undergone years of modifications without corresponding engineering documentation updates. Business impact accelerates as downtime costs accumulate. According to Fictiv’s MRO Strategy Guide , unplanned downtime costs manufacturers an average of $260,000 per hour, and emergency repairs can cost 3-10 times more than planned maintenance. The price of an obsolete part is often insignificant compared with the cost of an idle production line, missed delivery commitments, overtime labor, and expedited manufacturing or shipping. The longer an organization waits to deal with MRO parts obsolescence, the fewer sourcing options are available. What starts off as a manageable supply chain issue can evolve into a production emergency. This emergency is characterized by reactive panic buying, incomplete documentation, costly expedited shipping, and temporary workarounds that increase operational risk. When engineers recognize the obsolescence mismatch as a predictable lifecycle challenge early, rather than an isolated maintenance event, both downtime exposure and the total cost of sustaining aging manufacturing equipment can be reduced. Getting Ahead of the Obsolescence Gap The starting point is an obsolescence risk assessment—a structured review of critical components ranked by failure impact, lead time, and market availability. This surfaces the parts that pose the greatest operational risk, which are not always the most expensive ones: a low-cost bearing with a six-month lead time and no catalog alternative can stop a production line just as effectively as a failed drive. From there, the right strategy depends on where the equipment sits in its lifecycle—documentation and BOM accuracy for newer assets, reverse engineering and qualified manufacturing partners for aging ones, and pre-fabricated spare inventories for equipment approaching end of life. The organizations that manage obsolescence best are the ones that treat it as a predictable lifecycle challenge and build a supply strategy around it before the production line goes quiet. The MRO obsolescence mismatch refers to the gap between how long industrial equipment remains operational — typically 20–30 years — and how long its critical parts remain available through normal supply channels. Mechanical components can quietly disappear from supplier catalogs due to discontinued casting runs or supplier consolidation, while electronic and control components often follow a formal EOL timeline. In both cases, the equipment outlives its parts supply, creating sourcing challenges that grow more serious over time. How is mechanical parts obsolescence different from electronic parts obsolescence? Electronic and control components such as PLCs, drives, and HMIs typically follow a predictable support calendar, with formal EOL notices giving maintenance teams advance warning before parts move to last-time-buy status. Mechanical parts — bearings, gearboxes, hydraulic manifolds, structural castings — tend to disappear from the market more quietly, often with little or no formal notice. This makes mechanical obsolescence harder to anticipate and in some cases more operationally risky. When should manufacturers start planning for parts obsolescence? Ideally during the first five years of equipment life, when OEM support is fully available and parts are easy to source. This is the lowest-risk window to document complete BOMs, identify critical spare parts, and capture dimensional or CAD data for components that may eventually require reverse engineering. Waiting until parts become difficult to source — typically years six through ten — significantly narrows available options and increases both lead times and costs. What options are available when an OEM no longer supplies a critical part? When standard procurement channels are exhausted, maintenance and engineering teams typically have four options: locating remaining inventory through secondary or surplus suppliers; qualifying a compatible alternative part; commissioning a custom-fabricated replacement; or reverse engineering the original component using 3D scanning, CMM measurement, and CAD remodeling. The feasibility and cost of each option depends heavily on how complete the existing technical documentation is — gaps in drawings or BOMs can add significant time and cost before manufacturing can even begin. How much does unplanned downtime from parts obsolescence actually cost? The direct cost of an obsolete part is rarely the issue — the real cost is production downtime while sourcing, fabrication, or engineering workarounds are underway. Unplanned downtime costs manufacturers an average of $260,000 per hour, and emergency repairs typically cost three to ten times more than planned maintenance. When documentation is incomplete and parts require reverse engineering before they can be manufactured, those delays compound quickly, making proactive obsolescence planning one of the highest-return investments a maintenance organization can make.

Ideally during the first five years of equipment life, when OEM support is fully available and parts are easy to source. This is the lowest-risk window to document complete BOMs, identify critical spare parts, and capture dimensional or CAD data for components that may eventually require reverse engineering. Waiting until parts become difficult to source — typically years six through ten — significantly narrows available options and increases both lead times and costs. What options are available when an OEM no longer supplies a critical part? When standard procurement channels are exhausted, maintenance and engineering teams typically have four options: locating remaining inventory through secondary or surplus suppliers; qualifying a compatible alternative part; commissioning a custom-fabricated replacement; or reverse engineering the original component using 3D scanning, CMM measurement, and CAD remodeling. The feasibility and cost of each option depends heavily on how complete the existing technical documentation is — gaps in drawings or BOMs can add significant time and cost before manufacturing can even begin. How much does unplanned downtime from parts obsolescence actually cost? The direct cost of an obsolete part is rarely the issue — the real cost is production downtime while sourcing, fabrication, or engineering workarounds are underway. Unplanned downtime costs manufacturers an average of $260,000 per hour, and emergency repairs typically cost three to ten times more than planned maintenance. When documentation is incomplete and parts require reverse engineering before they can be manufactured, those delays compound quickly, making proactive obsolescence planning one of the highest-return investments a maintenance organization can make.

Be Part of the PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest! by: PCBWay Sep 03,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News We are glad to announce that PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest has arrived. Prior to this, PCBWay successfully held six design contests. In each contest, we saw many eye-catching projects shared by outstanding and creative electronic engineers and enthusiasts. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest will continue the previous purpose, which is to encourage more and more people to explore the charm of electronic design and participate in it. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . In this contest, in addition to the two themes of Electronic Project and Mechanical Project that have appeared before, we also introduced STM32 Project, hoping to give designers more room to perform. The contest will start on September 2nd, 2024, and project submissions will be accepted until January 19th, 2025. After this, the judging phase will begin, and the final winners will be announced on the PCBWay Blog on March 10th, 2025. Two ways to participate in the contest: Go to the contest page, find the Participate Now button and click it. In this case, the submitted project will automatically be entered into the competition; participants only need to select the theme of entry. Please note that if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. After filling in all the project information, simply click "Submit" at the bottom of the page. Go to the SharedProject Community ( https://www.pcbway.com/project/shareproject/ ) and click Create a project. Select the theme you are going to participate in. Similarly, if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. Hint: Sharing complete project files, including Gerber, BOM, Centroid file, schematics, 3D files, and so on will increase the chances of receiving a higher score. Awards and corresponding prizes: The First Prize : 1 winner, $1500 Cash + $200 Coupon + A Palm-sized Robot Dog*1 The Second Prize : 2 winners, $1000 Cash + $100 Coupon + Raspberry Pi 5 4GB *1 The Third Prize : 3 winners, $500 Cash + $50 Coupon + OpenMV4 H7 R2 Cam Smart Camera *1 Popular Design Prize : 10 winners, $100 Cash + $20 Coupon + $10 3D Printing Coupon + Multimeter ZTY890DPro *1 Participation Prize : Raspberry Pi Pico * 1 STM32 Great Project Prize : Six-Claw Multifunctional Aluminum Alloy Soldering Table *1 For more detailed information about the contest, please refer to: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . If there are any questions or suggestions, feel free to leave a comment below.We wish you the best of luck and look forward to your innovative designs! Verify Now Blog > Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay by: PCBWay May 30,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay recognizes the significant role it plays within the supply chain and broader society, along with the potential impact of its operations. To this end, we have established and strictly enforce the following principles, which not only govern our own conduct but also set clear expectations for our partners. Our goal is to ensure full legal and regulatory compliance, promote long-term sustainability, and generate a positive impact on society. Human Rights and Labor Protection No employment of individuals below the legal working age; all forms of forced or bonded labor are strictly prohibited. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace are not tolerated; an inclusive work environment for persons with disabilities is encouraged. Employees must be provided with fair compensation and reasonable rest periods, and their rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining must be respected. Business Ethics and Compliance Offering, promising, soliciting, or accepting any form of bribery is strictly prohibited; effective conflict of interest management and whistleblowing mechanisms must be in place. All financial and business records must accurately, completely, and truthfully reflect the underlying transactions. Full compliance with international sanctions, export controls, and other applicable laws and regulations is required. Supply Chain Responsibility and Sustainable Procurement PCBWay and its partners are required to extend the principles outlined in this document to all levels of entities within the supply chain. Priority should be given to selecting partners that are legally compliant, socially responsible, and committed to sustainable development. Identify social, labor, and environmental risks related to operations, and develop corresponding control and mitigation measures. Encourage partners to prioritize local sourcing to support regional economic development and job creation. Environmental Protection and Workplace Safety Actively implement environmental protection measures and continuously promote energy conservation and emission reduction; Ensure that all waste and hazardous materials are disposed of in accordance with relevant laws and regulations. The procurement or use of prohibited materials is not allowed. Provide employees with a safe working environment and health support mechanisms to prevent occupational injuries and health risks. PCBWay has fully adopted the DHL GoGreen transportation service in 2025 to reduce carbon emissions in the supply chain and promote the development of a green supply chain, with an initial target of reducing emissions by 30%. Information Protection and Transparent Governance Establish a comprehensive security system to strictly protect the confidentiality of customer data, drawings, and other business information. Comply with relevant laws and regulations to safeguard the personal data of customers and employees. Ensure that financial records are true, accurate, and complete, and prohibit any illegal activities. PCBWay will ensure the implementation of the above principles in actual cooperation and reserves the right to take action against any violations. The language of each individual Executive Order and Proclamation, as well as applicable Federal Register Notices, are dispositive as to the application of tariffs to imported products. Importers are responsible for exercising reasonable care in calculating applicable tariffs to their products based on all applicable legal authorities and correctly declaring the amount to CBP on entry documentation. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Update on June 24th Current Tax Rates for Various PCBWay Products Bare PCBs : 55% Stencils : 98% SMT Services : 45% CNC Machining : 65% Aluminum & Steel Components : 73% Plastic Components : 65% Other Products : 55% Note: The above tax rates are estimated for reference only, as tax rates are subject to significant real-time fluctuations. The dividing line between formal and informal customs declaration is 2500 In response to recent changes, we currently recommends the following logistics options: We advise using DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) logistics services with prepaid tariffs, such as: 1. DHL DTP (Duty & Tax Prepaid) , SF express If the item falls under HTS codes 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33, it qualifies for a 10% tariff exemption. However, DHL may incorrectly apply duties. If the recipient is charged duties despite the exemption, dispute it with DHL immediately—delays may invalidate the claim. DHL DTP will prepay customs duties & taxes. DHL may contact recipients for required documentation/clarification to clear shipments (regardless of Incoterm® used). When an individual or company purchases goods from an overseas supplier, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considers them the ultimate importer. The ultimate importer can clear the goods or have a Customs Broker clear them on their behalf. If the supplier hires a carrier that provides door to door service, the carrier service usually has brokers in their supply chain to clear the goods on behalf of the ultimate importer. If a formal entry is required, CBP regulations require the broker to put the ultimate importer's identification number on the CBP Form 7501- Entry Summary. The EIN is issued for the purpose of tax administration and are not intended for participation in any other activities (e.g., tax lien auction or sales, lotteries). For additional information about EIN, please visit the IRS web page "Apply for an Employer Identification (EIN) Online." Goods are usually cleared informally when they are for personal use, under $2500 in value, and are not in commercial quantities. A formal entry is usually required for commercial importations valued over $2,500. Because many foreign merchants are aware that CBP requires an identification number for the ultimate importer for formal entries, they will often request the purchaser's social security number to include on export documents that the broker will subsequently rely on to prepare the CBP entry. It should be noted that paperwork for goods sent by courier service does ask for an importer number, whether the import qualifies for an informal entry or not. Courier services file CBP entries electronically, and the software system they use requires an identification number to be provided for the recipient of the goods. If an identification number is not provided, the courier service is required to file a paper entry, which is extremely time-consuming and in the world of "Overnight Delivery" not practical. The end result is that most courier services will not accept packages for international delivery to U.S. residents if a recipient's identification number is not provided by the shipper. Goods sent through the international postal service that are under $2500 in value generally do not require an importer number to be cleared through CBP. (3) Effective June 1, 2025 at 12:01 AM EST: The flat tariff will increase to $200 $150 per item. 2. **Additional 125%+20% (If it is the category under 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33 , the tariff exemption is 125% ) 104% Tariff on High-value Chinese Goods** For Chinese-origin goods valued over $800: Effective April 9, 2025 at 12:01 AM EST: An additional tariff of 125% 104% will be applied to these products. 3.If the product falls under HTS categories 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33, it qualifies for a 125% tariff exemption. However, DHL’s customs declaration system may inaccurately apply or fail to recognize the 125% exemption. If the recipient finds that the product is indeed eligible for the exemption but the 125% duty relief was not applied, they must file a dispute with DHL immediately, as there is a strict deadline for appeals. By the time the sender notices the issue, the appeal window may have already closed. 4.Fedex Official: For B2C shipments, a valid FedEx account number is required. Note: All times mentioned are in U.S. Eastern Standard Time (EST). Regarding the latest US tariff policy, PCBWay will temporarily maintain the DDP/DTP charges unchanged. https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/04/amendment-to-recipricol-tariffs-and-updated-duties-as-applied-to-low-value-imports-from-the-peoples-republic-of-china/ Expected situation: If the category is under 9903.01.32 or 9903.01.33, the equivalent tariff is exempted by 125%： 20% (fentanyl) +25% (if 232 surcharges are involved) +25% (if 301 surcharges are involved) + exemption from equivalent tariffs + most-favored-nation rates ranging from 0% to 6.5%, with some combined rates reaching 45% to 76.5% Other: 20% (fentanyl) +125% equivalent tariff +25% (if 301 surcharge is involved) + most-favored-nation rates ranging from 0 to 6.5%, with some combined rates reaching 145% to 176.5% Note: 8471 is under the U.S. HS exemption code of 9903.01.32 and is not related to Section 232. The exemption scope of 9903.01.32 includes semiconductors, as well as some goods listed by the United States within the HS list. The applicable exemption scope of 9903.01.33 includes automobiles and some parts and components, and it is related to the Section 232 list. 9903.01.63 refers to goods other than those within the scopes of 9903.01.32 and 9903.01.33, and an additional 125% tariff will be imposed on them. =============================================================================================================================================== How Much Are Tariffs on Chinese Goods? It’s Trickier Than You Think. But because of an ever-changing patchwork of trade rules, not every product will be charged an astronomical tariff, trade lawyers, customs brokers and importers say. In some cases, tariffs will pile on other tariffs. In other instances, they can reduce costs, while other times they can cancel out new ones. The new 125 percent rate that President Trump imposed will in many cases be added on top of long-existing duties. There are four main categories of tariffs that are imposed on goods from China. Note: The tariff on auto parts comes into effect in early May. The average provided for the base rate is calculated by the World Trade Organization, which computes an average of all tariff lines. A large share of U.S. imports are assigned a 0% duty, but there are some very high rates in the tariff schedule. Rates ultimately depend on what is imported, what materials are used (from where), which special rates are applied and what sorts of products are exempt. New tariff rates on select goods from China Note: Rates are rounded to the nearest whole number. The rates are calculated assuming metal furniture made of 100 percent aluminum and door hinges made of 50 percent aluminum. Installation from the Official KiCad Repositories After installation, the plugin will appear on the right side of the navigation bar. And users can use it to export all the production files with just a click. Process demonstration： Sending the files to PCBWay, and they can be used for production after being reviewed by the staff. Note: If you want to place an assembly order, please be sure to add MPN information to the BOM. This can help the quoter source the devices you need more accurately. Manual installation Except for the way mentioned before, you can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Fabrication-Toolkit-for-KiCad: Open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About BOM Through BOM files, we can get all information of the components used in your design. In order to speed up the quotation process, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) If you have more suggestions, please leave a message below, PCBWay has committed to providing everyone with high-quality services. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Since we are not skilled enough to edit on github at the moment, any feedback or questions please contact with anson@pcbway.com Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Since we are not skilled enough to edit on github at the moment, any feedback or questions please contact with anson@pcbway.com Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for ProtoFlow PCBWay Plug-In for ProtoFlow by: PCBWay Oct 20,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News ProtoFlow is an AI-assisted PCB design tool for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It brings schematic capture, PCB layout and routing, and manufacturing file exports into one workspace. Users can describe a circuit in plain language to generate an editable schematic, then review, refine, and simulate the design. ProtoFlow also supports importing from and exporting to major EDA tools. Here is the link to ProtoFlow: https://www.protoflow.ai/ We’re excited to announce that PCBWay and ProtoFlow have teamed up to make the journey from PCB design to manufacturing easier. As AI continues to transform the way we work, ProtoFlow brings AI-assisted capabilities to PCB design, helping users design, simulate, and validate their boards before manufacturing. ProtoFlow takes PCBWay’s manufacturing requirements into account during the design process and checks the board for manufacturability before export, helping users identify and address potential issues early. Its built-in simulation tools and AI agent also allow users to test designs against their own requirements and refine them until all checks pass. Once the design is ready, users can send their Gerber, BOM, and coordinate files directly to PCBWay with just one click and go straight to the quotation page. This integration creates a smoother workflow from AI-assisted design to PCB manufacturing, helping makers and engineers turn their ideas into reality with greater ease: Ready to give it a try? Verify Now Blog > PCBWay and Tindie Launch the 2026 AI Hardware Design Contest PCBWay and Tindie Launch the 2026 AI Hardware Design Contest by: Mila Oct 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay is teaming up with Tindie to launch the 2026 AI Hardware Design Contest , inviting makers, engineers, developers, students, and hardware enthusiasts worldwide to explore the possibilities of combining artificial intelligence with hardware innovation. Whether you're building an AI-powered smart device, developing an intelligent embedded system, or experimenting with a creative DIY project, this is your opportunity to turn an idea into a working prototype<dynamic-value> your creation with the global maker community, and compete for a share of the $2,500 prize pool. Registration and project submissions open on November 1, 2026 (PT). Get your ideas ready and join the challenge! About the PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest Artificial intelligence is creating new possibilities for hardware development. From intelligent sensors and smart home devices to robotics and edge AI applications, AI is changing how electronic devices interact with people and the world around them. The PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest aims to encourage makers and developers to explore these possibilities through practical hardware projects. By combining PCBWay's PCB manufacturing and engineering capabilities with Tindie's hardware maker community, we hope to support innovative ideas and help more creators turn their concepts into real-world products. Whether you're an experienced hardware engineer or an independent maker exploring AI for the first time, you're welcome to participate. Project Ideas and Inspiration What can you build with AI and hardware? The possibilities are endless! You are free to choose your hardware, AI models, and deployment methods. There are no fixed competition tracks or restrictions on project direction. Here are eight areas to inspire your creativity: Vision Recognition Voice and Sound Environment and Smart Home Robotics and Control Edge AI / TinyML Wearables and Assistive Devices LLMs and Physical Interaction Creative Projects and Education These ideas are only starting points, not limitations. You can explore unconventional applications, combine multiple technologies, or develop an entirely different AI hardware concept. We encourage original thinking and creative approaches. How to Participate Joining the PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest involves five simple steps. Step 1. Register for the Contest Both individuals and teams are welcome to participate. Complete the official contest registration form. If you have purchased products on Tindie, you can optionally provide your Tindie order number to qualify for bonus points. Once your registration is successful, you will receive an official confirmation email. Step 2. Claim Your PCBWay Manufacturing Coupon To help participants bring their hardware ideas to life, PCBWay is offering 40 manufacturing coupons worth $50 each. Participants who need PCB fabrication or related manufacturing services can select the coupon option in the registration form. Each participant can claim one coupon only. Coupons are valid only during the contest period. The coupons are available in limited quantities, so remember to indicate your interest when registering. Step 3. Build Your AI Hardware Project Now it's time to turn your idea into a working creation! Choose your own hardware project and integrate AI-related functionality. Develop and complete a working physical prototype. Document your design, implementation, and demonstration process. Your project can use different hardware platforms, AI models, and deployment methods. What matters is that you create a functioning physical project with AI-related capabilities. Step 4. Publish and Submit Your Project Once your project is ready<dynamic-value> it with the community. Publish a complete project report on a public platform. Submit your project title, description, and report link through Tindie. A demonstration video is optional but encouraged. Your project report should clearly explain the concept, hardware design, AI implementation, development process, and final results. Step 5. Project Review and Awards After the submission deadline, PCBWay and Tindie will jointly review the entries and select the winning projects. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
