events.before: Resources / Materials / Nitriding: Definition, Process, and Application in Surface Hardening Nitriding: Definition, Process, and Application in Surface Hardening Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 25 min read Published July 16, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Nitriding is a thermochemical heat treatment process that diffuses nitrogen into the surface layer of metals to improve hardness, wear resistance, and fatigue performance. Nitriding operates below the transformation temperature of steel, from 480°C to 590°C, minimizing dimensional distortion compared to higher-temperature hardening methods. Nitrogen atoms penetrate the metal surface through diffusion, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, vanadium) to form hard nitride compounds within the surface layer. The nitride formation produces a hardened case depth ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, depending on the process duration and material composition. The industrial relevance of nitriding spans precision mechanical systems and high-load components across multiple manufacturing sectors. Gears, crankshafts, dies, molds, and aerospace structural components undergo nitriding to extend service life under cyclic loading and abrasive contact conditions. Surface hardness values achieved through nitriding range from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material and nitrogen source. Xometry provides nitriding services for components requiring controlled case depth, high surface hardness, and minimal distortion, making nitriding a reliable surface hardening solution for precision manufacturing applications. What Is Nitriding? Nitriding is a thermochemical diffusion process in which nitrogen atoms penetrate the surface of steel or alloy materials to create a hardened surface layer. The process introduces nitrogen rather than carbon, distinguishing it from carburizing and eliminating the need for quenching after treatment. Nitrogen diffuses into the metal surface at temperatures ranging from 480°C to 590°C, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) to form hard nitride compounds within the case layer. The absence of quenching reduces thermal shock and minimizes dimensional distortion, making nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tight dimensional tolerances. The hardened case produced by nitriding reaches surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material composition and process duration. Case depth ranges from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, providing a wear-resistant surface layer without altering the core mechanical properties of the base material. Nitriding applies to components (gears, crankshafts, dies, injection molds) that operate under cyclic loading, abrasive contact, and elevated temperature conditions across industrial and aerospace manufacturing environments. Why Does Nitrogen Improve Surface Hardness? Nitrogen improves surface hardness by reacting with alloying elements within the steel matrix to form hard nitride compounds throughout the diffused surface layer. Aluminum, chromium, and molybdenum present in the base material react with diffused nitrogen atoms to produce nitrides (AlN, CrN, Mo2N) that carry hardness values exceeding the base material. Aluminum nitride (AlN) reaches hardness values of 1,200 HV, chromium nitride (CrN) ranges from 1,000 HV to 1,100 HV, and molybdenum nitride (Mo2N) contributes hardness from 900 HV to 1,000 HV within the case layer. The nitride compounds distribute throughout the diffusion zone, creating a hardened network that resists plastic deformation under contact and abrasive loading. Steels with aluminum content from 0.85% to 1.5% produce the highest nitride density, making them preferred base materials for nitriding applications requiring maximum surface hardness. Does Nitriding Harden Only the Surface Layer? Yes, nitriding hardens only the surface layer. Nitrogen diffusion penetrates the metal to a controlled case depth ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, leaving the core mechanical properties of the base material unchanged. The hardened case carries surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, while the core retains its original toughness and ductility below the diffusion zone. A nitrided gear tooth carries a hard outer case that resists wear and contact fatigue, while the core absorbs impact loads without fracturing under cyclic operating conditions. The separation from surface hardness to core toughness makes nitriding suitable for components requiring wear resistance at the surface and structural integrity throughout the base material. How Does the Nitriding Process Work? The nitriding process works by exposing a prepared metal surface to a nitrogen-rich environment at controlled temperatures, driving nitrogen atoms into the surface layer through solid-state diffusion. Surface preparation begins with cleaning and degreasing the component to remove oxides, contaminants, and residual machining oils that inhibit nitrogen absorption. Components requiring selective hardening receive a copper or bronze plating mask on surfaces excluded from nitrogen diffusion. The prepared component enters a furnace or reaction vessel, where the temperature rises to the nitriding range from 480°C to 590°C. Nitrogen introduced at the nitriding temperature diffuses into the metal surface, reacting with alloying elements to form hard nitride compounds within the growing case layer. The diffusion rate and case depth depend on temperature, treatment duration, and base material composition, with case depths reaching from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment times from 10 hours to 130 hours. Controlled cooling follows nitrogen diffusion, returning the component to ambient temperature without quenching. The absence of quenching preserves dimensional stability, making nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tight tolerances after surface hardening. What Happens During Nitrogen Diffusion in Nitriding? Nitrogen diffusion begins when atomic nitrogen generated at the metal surface migrates inward through the crystal lattice of the base material. The nitrogen atoms occupy interstitial positions within the iron matrix, moving progressively deeper into the surface layer as the treatment continues. Nitrogen reacts with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) present in the steel matrix, forming hard nitride compounds (AlN, CrN, Mo2N) distributed throughout the diffusion zone. The nitride compounds accumulate nearest to the surface, producing a compound layer from 0.01 mm to 0.03 mm thick, followed by a deeper diffusion zone extending to 0.65 mm. The diffusion rate depends on temperature, treatment duration, and alloying element concentration within the base material. Higher treatment temperatures accelerate nitrogen migration but reduce surface hardness by altering nitride distribution within the case layer. A treatment temperature of 520°C over 48 hours produces a case depth of 0.3 mm in chromium-alloyed steels, balancing diffusion depth against surface hardness retention. Why Is Nitriding Performed Below the Austenitizing Temperature? Nitriding is performed below the austenitizing temperature to prevent phase transformation in the steel matrix, preserving dimensional stability and core mechanical properties throughout the treatment. The austenitizing temperature of steel ranges from 720°C to 900°C, depending on the alloy composition, while nitriding operates from 480°C to 590°C, staying well below the transformation threshold. Operating below the austenitizing temperature eliminates the need for quenching after treatment, removing the primary source of dimensional distortion in conventional hardening processes. A nitrided crankshaft retains its ground dimensions within 0.025 mm after treatment, confirming the dimensional stability that the sub-transformation temperature range provides for precision components requiring tight tolerances after surface hardening. What Are the Main Types of Nitriding Processes? The main types of nitriding processes are listed below. Gas Nitriding : Gas nitriding exposes the component to an ammonia (NH3) atmosphere at temperatures from 490°C to 530°C, dissociating ammonia into atomic nitrogen and hydrogen at the metal surface. The atomic nitrogen diffuses into the surface layer, producing case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment times from 10 hours to 130 hours. Plasma Nitriding : Plasma nitriding uses an electrical discharge in a low-pressure nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture to generate ionized nitrogen that bombards and diffuses into the metal surface. The process operates from 350°C to 570°C, producing precise case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm with a superior surface finish compared to gas nitriding. Salt Bath Nitriding : Salt bath nitriding immerses the component in a molten cyanide or cyanate salt bath at temperatures from 510°C to 580°C, transferring nitrogen and carbon simultaneously into the surface layer. The process produces case depths from 0.01 mm to 0.3 mm within treatment times from 1 hour to 4 hours, making it the fastest nitriding method. Ion Nitriding : Ion nitriding applies a high-voltage electrical field in a vacuum chamber containing nitrogen gas, accelerating nitrogen ions directly into the metal surface at temperatures from 350°C to 600°C. The process delivers precise control over compound layer composition and thickness, producing case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.5 mm with minimal surface distortion across precision aerospace and tooling components. How Does Gas Nitriding Work? Gas nitriding works by exposing steel components to an ammonia-rich furnace atmosphere at temperatures from 490°C to 530°C, where ammonia dissociates into atomic nitrogen and hydrogen at the metal surface. The dissociation rate of ammonia controls the nitrogen potential at the surface, determining the concentration of nitrogen available for diffusion into the base material. Atomic nitrogen migrates into the steel matrix, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) to form hard nitride compounds throughout the developing case layer. The furnace atmosphere maintains a controlled ammonia dissociation rate from 15% to 30%, regulating nitrogen supply across the full treatment duration. Case depth increases progressively with treatment time, reaching from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment durations from 10 hours to 130 hours. Surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV develop across the case layer, depending on the alloying element concentration in the base material. Gas nitriding suits high-volume production of components (gears, crankshafts, camshafts) requiring consistent case depth and surface hardness across large batch quantities. Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo "The true value of sub-critical thermochemical processing lies in the clean separation of core toughness from surface wear performance. By optimizing Design for Manufacturing (DFM) selections to favor predictable diffusion layers, engineers can completely bypass the highly disruptive post-hardening grinding operations that typically distort geometric tolerances. Achieving this type of processing harmony represents a critical milestone where surface optimization directly preserves the structural intent of the component." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering How Does Plasma Nitriding Differ From Gas Nitriding? Plasma nitriding differs from gas nitriding by using an electrical discharge in a low-pressure nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture to generate ionized nitrogen, rather than relying on ammonia dissociation at atmospheric pressure. The electrical discharge creates a plasma zone surrounding the component, accelerating nitrogen ions directly into the metal surface at temperatures from 350°C to 570°C. The lower operating temperature reduces thermal distortion compared to gas nitriding, making plasma nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tighter dimensional tolerances after treatment. Plasma nitriding provides superior process control by adjusting the nitrogen-to-hydrogen gas ratio, voltage, and pressure independently to regulate compound layer composition and case depth. A nitrogen-to-hydrogen ratio from 1:4 to 1:9 controls the formation of epsilon and gamma-prime nitride phases within the compound layer, allowing metallurgists to tailor surface properties for specific applications (cutting tools, injection molds, aerospace structural components). Is Plasma Nitriding More Precise Than Conventional Gas Nitriding? Yes, plasma nitriding is more precise than conventional gas nitriding. Plasma nitriding controls compound layer thickness from 0.001 mm to 0.02 mm by adjusting the nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture ratio, treatment temperature, and electrical discharge parameters during processing. Gas nitriding relies on ammonia dissociation rates from 15% to 30% to regulate nitrogen supply, producing less consistent compound layer control across complex component geometries. Plasma nitriding operates at lower temperatures from 350°C to 570°C, reducing thermal distortion on precision components requiring dimensional tolerances within 0.025 mm after treatment. The localized surface activation in plasma nitriding allows selective hardening of specific surface areas without masking, reducing preparation time compared to gas nitriding processes that require physical masking for selective treatment. What Materials Are Suitable for Nitriding? The materials that are suitable for nitriding are listed below. Alloy Steels : Alloy steels containing chromium, molybdenum, and vanadium respond effectively to nitriding by forming dense nitride distributions throughout the case layer. Grades (4140, 4340, 8640) reach surface hardness values from 650 HV to 900 HV after nitriding, making them suitable for gears, crankshafts, and high-load structural components. Nitriding Steels : Nitriding steels carry aluminum content from 0.85% to 1.5%, producing the highest nitride density and surface hardness values from 900 HV to 1,200 HV across the treated case layer. Grade EN 41B is a widely used nitriding steel, delivering consistent case depths from 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm across precision aerospace and automotive components. Tool Steels : Tool steels (H13, D2, M2) undergo nitriding to extend service life under abrasive contact and thermal cycling conditions in dies, molds, and cutting tools. Nitrided tool steel surfaces reach hardness values from 900 HV to 1,100 HV, reducing wear rates and extending tool service intervals in high-volume production environments. Stainless Steels : Stainless steels require specialized nitriding conditions because the passive chromium oxide layer on the surface inhibits nitrogen diffusion under standard treatment parameters. Low-temperature plasma nitriding from 350°C to 450°C activates the stainless steel surface without destroying corrosion resistance, producing case depths from 0.01 mm to 0.02 mm on austenitic grades (316L, 304). Titanium Alloys : Titanium alloys undergo nitriding at temperatures from 700°C to 1,000°C, forming titanium nitride (TiN) surface layers that reach hardness values from 1,800 HV to 2,400 HV. Grade Ti-6Al-4V produces a golden TiN compound layer from 0.001 mm to 0.01 mm thick, improving wear resistance across aerospace and biomedical implant applications. Why Are Alloy Steels Commonly Used in Nitriding? Alloy steels are commonly used in nitriding because chromium, aluminum, and molybdenum present in the steel matrix react readily with diffused nitrogen atoms to form hard nitride compounds throughout the case layer. The nitride-forming alloying elements produce dense nitride distributions that raise surface hardness values from 650 HV to 900 HV, exceeding the hardness achievable in plain carbon steels under identical nitriding conditions. Chromium content from 0.7% to 1.1 % in alloy steel grades (4140, 4340) produces consistent chromium nitride (CrN) distributions, delivering reliable case depths from 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm across treated components. Molybdenum content from 0.15% to 0.4% contributes additional nitride formation, raising core toughness and reducing brittleness within the hardened case layer. Aluminum content from 0.85% to 1.5% produces the highest nitride density among common alloying elements, generating surface hardness values of 1,200 HV in dedicated nitriding grades. The combination of multiple nitride-forming elements in Alloy Steels makes them the most consistently responsive material class for industrial nitriding applications. Can Plain Carbon Steels Be Nitrided Effectively? No, plain carbon steels cannot be nitrided effectively. The absence of nitride-forming alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) prevents dense nitride distributions from developing within the case layer. Nitrogen diffuses into the steel matrix but reacts with iron, forming iron nitrides (Fe2N, Fe3N, Fe4N) that carry hardness values from 250 HV to 400 HV, significantly lower than the 650 HV to 1,200 HV achieved in alloy steel grades. The iron nitride compounds produce a brittle compound layer that fractures under cyclic loading and abrasive contact conditions, limiting functional performance across precision manufacturing environments. Alloy steel grades with chromium, aluminum, and molybdenum content remain the preferred material selection for nitriding applications requiring consistent surface hardness and wear resistance, compared to Plain Carbon Steels . What Mechanical Properties Change During Nitriding? The mechanical properties that change during nitriding are listed below. Surface Hardness Increase : Nitriding raises surface hardness by forming hard nitride compounds (AlN, CrN, Mo2N) throughout the case layer during nitrogen diffusion. Surface hardness values increase from a pre-treatment range of 200 HV to 350 HV to 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material composition and treatment parameters. Improved Wear Resistance : The hardened nitride case layer resists abrasive and adhesive wear under contact loading conditions, extending component service life across high-load applications. Nitrided gear surfaces demonstrate wear rates to 10 times lower than untreated alloy steel surfaces operating under identical contact stress conditions. Improved Fatigue Strength : Nitriding introduces compressive residual stresses into the surface layer, raising the fatigue strength of treated components by 20% to 40% compared to untreated base material. The compressive stress layer counteracts tensile fatigue stresses generated at the surface during cyclic loading, delaying crack initiation across rotating and reciprocating components. Better Corrosion Resistance : Nitrided stainless steel and aluminum-bearing alloy grades develop a dense nitride surface layer that reduces oxidation and corrosion rates in moderate chemical environments. Plasma-nitrided austenitic stainless steel grades (316L, 304) retain corrosion resistance while achieving surface hardness values from 1,000 HV to 1,200 HV at low treatment temperatures from 350°C to 450°C. Reduced Friction Behavior : The compound layer formed during nitriding reduces the surface friction coefficient from 0.6 to 0.8 in untreated steel down to 0.1 to 0.3 in nitrided surfaces under dry sliding conditions. The lower friction coefficient reduces heat generation and adhesive wear at contact interfaces, improving operational efficiency in sliding and rotating component applications. How Does Nitriding Improve Fatigue Resistance? Nitriding improves fatigue resistance by introducing compressive residual stresses into the surface layer during nitrogen diffusion and nitride formation. The compressive stress layer counteracts tensile fatigue stresses generated at the component surface under cyclic loading, delaying crack initiation at stress concentration points (notches, fillets, surface defects). Compressive residual stress values from 200 MPa to 800 MPa develop within the nitrided case layer, depending on the base material composition and treatment parameters. Rotating components (crankshafts, camshafts, gear shafts) benefit directly from the combined effect of compressive stress and surface hardness, raising fatigue strength by 20% to 40% compared to untreated base material. A nitrided crankshaft operating at cyclic bending stresses of 400 MPa demonstrates fatigue life improvements exceeding 50% compared to an untreated equivalent, confirming the measurable fatigue resistance gains nitriding delivers across precision rotating components. Does Nitriding Improve Corrosion Resistance? Yes, nitriding improves corrosion resistance. The compound layer formed during nitriding creates a dense nitrogen-rich surface that reduces oxidation and corrosion rates in moderate chemical environments. Plasma-nitrided austenitic stainless steel grades (316L, 304) retain corrosion resistance while achieving surface hardness values from 1,000 HV to 1,200 HV at treatment temperatures from 350°C to 450°C. Gas nitriding at temperatures exceeding 550°C reduces corrosion resistance in stainless steel grades by depleting chromium from the matrix through chromium nitride formation. Aluminum-bearing nitriding steels develop a dense aluminum nitride (AlN) surface layer that provides moderate corrosion protection in dry and low-humidity industrial environments. What Equipment Is Used in Nitriding? The equipment that is used in nitriding is listed below. Controlled Atmosphere Furnaces : Sealed furnaces maintain a consistent ammonia-rich environment at temperatures from 490°C to 530°C throughout the gas nitriding treatment cycle. Ammonia dissociation rates from 15% to 30% are regulated to control nitrogen supply and case depth development across batch quantities of components. Plasma Nitriding Chambers : Low-pressure vessels operating from 1 mbar to 10 mbar generate an electrical discharge in a nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture to produce ionized nitrogen at the component surface. The chambers accommodate component sizes from small precision parts to large structural components to 2,000 mm in diameter, depending on chamber dimensions. Vacuum Systems : Evacuated enclosures reach base pressures from 0.01 mbar to 0.1 mbar before introducing the nitriding gas mixture, eliminating residual oxygen that inhibits nitrogen diffusion at the metal surface. Roots blowers and rotary vane pumps or dry screw pumps maintain the required vacuum levels throughout the treatment cycle. Gas Flow Control Systems : Networked mass flow controllers regulate the supply of ammonia, nitrogen, and hydrogen into the treatment chamber, maintaining precise gas mixture ratios throughout the nitriding cycle. Real-time adjustments ensure consistent nitrogen potential at the component surface across the full treatment duration. Temperature Monitoring Systems : Thermocouples and pyrometers measure and regulate furnace temperature within ±5°C of the target nitriding range from 480°C to 590°C. Precise temperature control ensures consistent nitrogen diffusion rates and case depth development across all components within the treatment batch. How Do Furnaces Control Nitrogen Activity During Nitriding? Furnaces control nitrogen activity during nitriding by regulating the ammonia dissociation rate within the treatment chamber atmosphere. Ammonia (NH3) introduced into the furnace dissociates into atomic nitrogen and hydrogen at the heated metal surface, with the dissociation rate determining the concentration of nitrogen available for diffusion. A dissociation rate from 15% to 30% maintains high nitrogen activity at the surface, producing consistent case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across the treatment batch. Mass flow controllers adjust ammonia supply in real time, compensating for temperature fluctuations that alter dissociation rates during the treatment cycle. Higher dissociation rates above 85% reduce nitrogen activity at the surface, accelerating case depth development while lowering surface hardness values across treated components. Furnace atmosphere analyzers measure hydrogen content within the chamber to calculate the actual dissociation rate, allowing operators to maintain nitrogen activity within the target range throughout the full treatment duration. Does Nitriding Require Quenching After Treatment? No, nitriding does not require quenching after treatment. The process operates below the austenitizing temperature of steel, from 480°C to 590°C, preventing phase transformation in the steel matrix that otherwise necessitates rapid cooling. Controlled cooling returns the component to ambient temperature slowly within the furnace atmosphere, preserving the dimensional stability achieved during treatment. A nitrided crankshaft retains ground dimensions within 0.025 mm after treatment, confirming that the absence of quenching eliminates the primary source of distortion present in conventional hardening processes. Components requiring tight dimensional tolerances after surface hardening benefit directly from the distortion-free cooling sequence that nitriding provides across precision manufacturing environments. What Are the Applications of Nitriding The applications of nitriding are listed below. Automotive Crankshafts : Nitriding extends crankshaft service life by producing a hardened case layer that resists wear and fatigue under cyclic bending and torsional loading conditions. Surface hardness values from 650 HV to 900 HV develop across the journal surfaces, reducing wear rates and extending service intervals in high-output engine applications. Gears and Camshafts : Gear tooth surfaces and camshaft lobes undergo nitriding to resist contact fatigue and abrasive wear under high-cycle loading conditions. The compressive residual stress layer raises fatigue strength by 20% to 40%, extending service life across transmission and valvetrain components operating under continuous cyclic stress. Injection Molds and Dies : Mold cavities and die surfaces reach surface hardness values from 900 HV to 1,100 HV after nitriding, resisting abrasive wear from filled polymer materials and repeated thermal cycling. The hardened surface extends mold service life beyond 500,000 cycles in high-volume injection molding production environments. Aerospace Components : Structural aerospace parts (landing gear components, actuator shafts, turbine accessory shafts) undergo nitriding to achieve surface hardness and fatigue resistance under high-stress operating conditions. Dimensional distortion remains within 0.025 mm after treatment, preserving the tight tolerances required across precision aerospace assemblies. Industrial Tooling : Cutting tools, broaches, and forming dies undergo nitriding to extend tool life under abrasive contact and high-pressure forming conditions. Nitrided tool surfaces reach hardness values from 900 HV to 1,100 HV, reducing tool replacement frequency and lowering per-unit production costs across high-volume manufacturing operations. Hydraulic System Parts : Hydraulic cylinder rods, valve spools, and pump components undergo nitriding to resist wear and corrosion under high-pressure fluid contact conditions. The nitrided surface layer reduces friction coefficients from 0.6 to 0.1 to 0.3, improving sealing performance and extending component service life in hydraulic systems operating at pressures from 200 bar to 400 bar. Why Is Nitriding Important for Tooling Applications? Nitriding is important for tooling applications because it improves wear resistance and surface durability in tools exposed to repeated contact stress and abrasive loading conditions. Cutting tools, broaches, and forming dies develop surface hardness values from 900 HV to 1,100 HV after nitriding, resisting material removal and surface degradation under high-cycle operating conditions. The hardened nitride case layer reduces wear rates by up to 10 times compared to untreated tool steel surfaces, extending service intervals and reducing replacement frequency across high-volume production environments. Compressive residual stresses introduced during nitriding raise fatigue strength by 20% to 40%, preventing crack initiation at stress concentration points (cutting edges, die radii, forming surfaces) under repeated contact loading. Tool steels (H13, D2, M2) respond effectively to nitriding, reaching case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm that provide durable wear resistance without altering core toughness across precision tooling applications. Are Aerospace Components Commonly Nitrided? Yes, aerospace components are commonly nitrided. Structural parts (landing gear components, actuator shafts, turbine accessory shafts) undergo nitriding to achieve surface hardness and fatigue resistance under high-stress operating conditions. Surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV develop across treated aerospace surfaces, depending on the base material composition and nitriding process applied. Compressive residual stresses from 200 MPa to 800 MPa introduced during nitriding raise fatigue strength by 20% to 40%, extending service life across components operating under continuous cyclic loading. Dimensional distortion remains within 0.025 mm after treatment, preserving the tight tolerances required across precision aerospace assemblies where dimensional accuracy directly affects structural performance and safety certification requirements. How Does Nitriding Compare to Carburizing? Nitriding and carburizing are thermochemical diffusion processes that harden the surface layer of steel components, but differ fundamentally in diffusing element, process temperature, and post-treatment requirements. Nitriding diffuses nitrogen into the steel surface at temperatures from 480°C to 590°C, while carburizing diffuses carbon at higher temperatures from 850°C to 950°C. Nitriding operates below the austenitizing temperature, eliminating the need for quenching after treatment and preserving dimensional stability within 0.025 mm. Carburizing requires quenching after carbon diffusion to transform the austenitic case into martensite, introducing dimensional distortion that necessitates post-treatment grinding on precision components. The hardened case produced by nitriding reaches surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV at case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, while carburizing produces surface hardness values from 550 HV to 850 HV at deeper case depths from 0.5 mm to 4.0 mm. Nitriding suits precision components (gears, crankshafts, dies) requiring tight dimensional tolerances and high surface hardness after treatment. Carburizing suits heavy-load components requiring deeper case depths and higher core toughness under impact loading conditions, making the selection from nitriding to carburizing dependent on the functional requirements of the application. What Is the Difference Between Nitriding and Carburizing? Nitriding and carburizing differ in the diffusing element, process temperature, and post-treatment requirements applied to harden the surface layer of steel components. Nitriding diffuses nitrogen into the steel surface at temperatures from 480°C to 590°C, while carburizing diffuses carbon at temperatures from 850°C to 950°C, requiring the steel matrix to reach the austenitic phase. Nitriding eliminates the need for quenching after treatment, preserving dimensional stability within 0.025 mm across precision components. Carburizing requires quenching to transform the carbon-enriched austenitic case into martensite, introducing dimensional distortion that necessitates post-treatment grinding. The nitrided case reaches surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV at depths from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, while the carburized case produces hardness values from 550 HV to 850 HV at deeper case depths from 0.5 mm to 4.0 mm. Nitriding suits precision components requiring tight tolerances, while carburizing suits heavy-load applications requiring deeper case penetration and higher impact resistance. Is Nitriding Less Distortive Than Carburizing? Yes, nitriding is less distortive than carburizing. Nitriding operates below the austenitizing temperature of steel, from 480°C to 590°C, preventing phase transformation in the steel matrix and eliminating the need for quenching after treatment. Carburizing operates from 850°C to 950°C, requiring quenching to transform the austenitic case into martensite, generating thermal gradients that produce dimensional distortion across treated components. Nitrided components retain ground dimensions within 0.025 mm after treatment, while carburized components require post-treatment grinding to restore dimensional accuracy lost during quenching. Precision components (crankshafts, injection mold cavities, hydraulic valve spools) requiring tight dimensional tolerances after surface hardening favor nitriding over carburizing to avoid the distortion and additional processing costs associated with post-quench grinding operations. What Are the Limitations of Nitriding? Nitriding carries process limitations that affect its suitability across different manufacturing applications. Processing times from 10 hours to 130 hours make gas nitriding significantly slower than carburizing, which achieves much deeper case depths in 4 hours to 12 hours at higher treatment temperatures. Case depth remains limited from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, restricting nitriding to applications where shallow surface hardening meets the functional requirement. Components requiring case depths exceeding 1.0 mm for heavy impact or deep abrasive wear resistance fall outside the practical range of nitriding as a surface hardening solution. Alloy dependency presents a further constraint, as plain carbon steels and low-alloy grades produce iron nitrides with hardness values from 250 HV to 400 HV, significantly below the 650 HV to 1,200 HV achieved in chromium and aluminum-bearing alloy steels. Equipment costs for plasma nitriding chambers and vacuum systems range from $150,000 to $500,000, raising the capital investment threshold for in-house nitriding operations. Salt bath nitriding introduces cyanide-bearing waste streams requiring specialized disposal procedures, adding environmental compliance costs to the process expenditure. Why Is Nitriding Slower Than Some Other Surface Hardening Processes? Nitriding is slower than some other surface hardening processes because nitrogen diffusion through the steel matrix occurs at a lower rate than carbon diffusion in carburizing. The process operates from 480°C to 590°C, significantly below the 850°C to 950°C range used in carburizing, reducing atomic mobility and slowing diffusion rate across the developing case layer. Achieving a case depth of 0.3 mm through gas nitriding requires treatment times from 24 hours to 48 hours, while carburizing reaches comparable depths in less than 1 hour at higher treatment temperatures. Increasing the nitriding temperature accelerates nitrogen diffusion but reduces surface hardness by altering nitride distribution within the case layer, limiting the practical upper temperature boundary of the process. Treatment times from 10 hours to 130 hours reflect the extended duration nitrogen diffusion requires to develop sufficient case depth across alloy steel components in industrial nitriding applications. Can Improper Nitriding Cause Brittle Surface Layers? Yes, improper nitriding can cause brittle surface layers. Excessive nitrogen activity at the metal surface produces a thick compound layer exceeding 0.03 mm, generating a brittle white layer that fractures under contact and impact loading conditions. Ammonia dissociation rates falling below 15% increase nitrogen concentration at the surface, accelerating compound layer growth beyond the functional thickness range. A compound layer exceeding 0.05 mm demonstrates brittleness under cyclic loading, initiating surface cracks that propagate into the diffusion zone beneath the hardened case. Overnitriding at temperatures below 480°C reduces nitrogen diffusion depth, concentrating nitride formation at the immediate surface and producing a shallow, brittle case layer with reduced fatigue resistance. Post-nitriding compound layer thickness measurements using metallographic cross-sections confirm whether the white layer remains within the acceptable range from 0.01 mm to 0.03 mm across precision components. Nitriding operates below the transformation temperature of steel, from 480°C to 590°C, minimizing dimensional distortion compared to higher-temperature hardening methods. Nitrogen atoms penetrate the metal surface through diffusion, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum, vanadium) to form hard nitride compounds within the surface layer. The nitride formation produces a hardened case depth ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, depending on the process duration and material composition. The industrial relevance of nitriding spans precision mechanical systems and high-load components across multiple manufacturing sectors. Gears, crankshafts, dies, molds, and aerospace structural components undergo nitriding to extend service life under cyclic loading and abrasive contact conditions. Surface hardness values achieved through nitriding range from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material and nitrogen source. Xometry provides nitriding services for components requiring controlled case depth, high surface hardness, and minimal distortion, making nitriding a reliable surface hardening solution for precision manufacturing applications. What Is Nitriding? Nitriding is a thermochemical diffusion process in which nitrogen atoms penetrate the surface of steel or alloy materials to create a hardened surface layer. The process introduces nitrogen rather than carbon, distinguishing it from carburizing and eliminating the need for quenching after treatment. Nitrogen diffuses into the metal surface at temperatures ranging from 480°C to 590°C, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) to form hard nitride compounds within the case layer. The absence of quenching reduces thermal shock and minimizes dimensional distortion, making nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tight dimensional tolerances. The hardened case produced by nitriding reaches surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material composition and process duration. Case depth ranges from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, providing a wear-resistant surface layer without altering the core mechanical properties of the base material. Nitriding applies to components (gears, crankshafts, dies, injection molds) that operate under cyclic loading, abrasive contact, and elevated temperature conditions across industrial and aerospace manufacturing environments. Why Does Nitrogen Improve Surface Hardness? Nitrogen improves surface hardness by reacting with alloying elements within the steel matrix to form hard nitride compounds throughout the diffused surface layer. Aluminum, chromium, and molybdenum present in the base material react with diffused nitrogen atoms to produce nitrides (AlN, CrN, Mo2N) that carry hardness values exceeding the base material. Aluminum nitride (AlN) reaches hardness values of 1,200 HV, chromium nitride (CrN) ranges from 1,000 HV to 1,100 HV, and molybdenum nitride (Mo2N) contributes hardness from 900 HV to 1,000 HV within the case layer. The nitride compounds distribute throughout the diffusion zone, creating a hardened network that resists plastic deformation under contact and abrasive loading. Steels with aluminum content from 0.85% to 1.5% produce the highest nitride density, making them preferred base materials for nitriding applications requiring maximum surface hardness. Does Nitriding Harden Only the Surface Layer? Yes, nitriding hardens only the surface layer. Nitrogen diffusion penetrates the metal to a controlled case depth ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm, leaving the core mechanical properties of the base material unchanged. The hardened case carries surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV, while the core retains its original toughness and ductility below the diffusion zone. A nitrided gear tooth carries a hard outer case that resists wear and contact fatigue, while the core absorbs impact loads without fracturing under cyclic operating conditions. The separation from surface hardness to core toughness makes nitriding suitable for components requiring wear resistance at the surface and structural integrity throughout the base material. How Does the Nitriding Process Work? The nitriding process works by exposing a prepared metal surface to a nitrogen-rich environment at controlled temperatures, driving nitrogen atoms into the surface layer through solid-state diffusion. Surface preparation begins with cleaning and degreasing the component to remove oxides, contaminants, and residual machining oils that inhibit nitrogen absorption. Components requiring selective hardening receive a copper or bronze plating mask on surfaces excluded from nitrogen diffusion. The prepared component enters a furnace or reaction vessel, where the temperature rises to the nitriding range from 480°C to 590°C. Nitrogen introduced at the nitriding temperature diffuses into the metal surface, reacting with alloying elements to form hard nitride compounds within the growing case layer. The diffusion rate and case depth depend on temperature, treatment duration, and base material composition, with case depths reaching from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment times from 10 hours to 130 hours. Controlled cooling follows nitrogen diffusion, returning the component to ambient temperature without quenching. The absence of quenching preserves dimensional stability, making nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tight tolerances after surface hardening. What Happens During Nitrogen Diffusion in Nitriding? Nitrogen diffusion begins when atomic nitrogen generated at the metal surface migrates inward through the crystal lattice of the base material. The nitrogen atoms occupy interstitial positions within the iron matrix, moving progressively deeper into the surface layer as the treatment continues. Nitrogen reacts with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) present in the steel matrix, forming hard nitride compounds (AlN, CrN, Mo2N) distributed throughout the diffusion zone. The nitride compounds accumulate nearest to the surface, producing a compound layer from 0.01 mm to 0.03 mm thick, followed by a deeper diffusion zone extending to 0.65 mm. The diffusion rate depends on temperature, treatment duration, and alloying element concentration within the base material. Higher treatment temperatures accelerate nitrogen migration but reduce surface hardness by altering nitride distribution within the case layer. A treatment temperature of 520°C over 48 hours produces a case depth of 0.3 mm in chromium-alloyed steels, balancing diffusion depth against surface hardness retention. Why Is Nitriding Performed Below the Austenitizing Temperature? Nitriding is performed below the austenitizing temperature to prevent phase transformation in the steel matrix, preserving dimensional stability and core mechanical properties throughout the treatment. The austenitizing temperature of steel ranges from 720°C to 900°C, depending on the alloy composition, while nitriding operates from 480°C to 590°C, staying well below the transformation threshold. Operating below the austenitizing temperature eliminates the need for quenching after treatment, removing the primary source of dimensional distortion in conventional hardening processes. A nitrided crankshaft retains its ground dimensions within 0.025 mm after treatment, confirming the dimensional stability that the sub-transformation temperature range provides for precision components requiring tight tolerances after surface hardening. What Are the Main Types of Nitriding Processes? The main types of nitriding processes are listed below. Gas Nitriding : Gas nitriding exposes the component to an ammonia (NH3) atmosphere at temperatures from 490°C to 530°C, dissociating ammonia into atomic nitrogen and hydrogen at the metal surface. The atomic nitrogen diffuses into the surface layer, producing case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment times from 10 hours to 130 hours. Plasma Nitriding : Plasma nitriding uses an electrical discharge in a low-pressure nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture to generate ionized nitrogen that bombards and diffuses into the metal surface. The process operates from 350°C to 570°C, producing precise case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm with a superior surface finish compared to gas nitriding. Salt Bath Nitriding : Salt bath nitriding immerses the component in a molten cyanide or cyanate salt bath at temperatures from 510°C to 580°C, transferring nitrogen and carbon simultaneously into the surface layer. The process produces case depths from 0.01 mm to 0.3 mm within treatment times from 1 hour to 4 hours, making it the fastest nitriding method. Ion Nitriding : Ion nitriding applies a high-voltage electrical field in a vacuum chamber containing nitrogen gas, accelerating nitrogen ions directly into the metal surface at temperatures from 350°C to 600°C. The process delivers precise control over compound layer composition and thickness, producing case depths from 0.1 mm to 0.5 mm with minimal surface distortion across precision aerospace and tooling components. How Does Gas Nitriding Work? Gas nitriding works by exposing steel components to an ammonia-rich furnace atmosphere at temperatures from 490°C to 530°C, where ammonia dissociates into atomic nitrogen and hydrogen at the metal surface. The dissociation rate of ammonia controls the nitrogen potential at the surface, determining the concentration of nitrogen available for diffusion into the base material. Atomic nitrogen migrates into the steel matrix, reacting with alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) to form hard nitride compounds throughout the developing case layer. The furnace atmosphere maintains a controlled ammonia dissociation rate from 15% to 30%, regulating nitrogen supply across the full treatment duration. Case depth increases progressively with treatment time, reaching from 0.1 mm to 0.65 mm across treatment durations from 10 hours to 130 hours. Surface hardness values from 650 HV to 1,200 HV develop across the case layer, depending on the alloying element concentration in the base material. Gas nitriding suits high-volume production of components (gears, crankshafts, camshafts) requiring consistent case depth and surface hardness across large batch quantities. Plasma nitriding differs from gas nitriding by using an electrical discharge in a low-pressure nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture to generate ionized nitrogen, rather than relying on ammonia dissociation at atmospheric pressure. The electrical discharge creates a plasma zone surrounding the component, accelerating nitrogen ions directly into the metal surface at temperatures from 350°C to 570°C. The lower operating temperature reduces thermal distortion compared to gas nitriding, making plasma nitriding suitable for precision components requiring tighter dimensional tolerances after treatment. Plasma nitriding provides superior process control by adjusting the nitrogen-to-hydrogen gas ratio, voltage, and pressure independently to regulate compound layer composition and case depth. A nitrogen-to-hydrogen ratio from 1:4 to 1:9 controls the formation of epsilon and gamma-prime nitride phases within the compound layer, allowing metallurgists to tailor surface properties for specific applications (cutting tools, injection molds, aerospace structural components). Is Plasma Nitriding More Precise Than Conventional Gas Nitriding? Yes, plasma nitriding is more precise than conventional gas nitriding. Plasma nitriding controls compound layer thickness from 0.001 mm to 0.02 mm by adjusting the nitrogen and hydrogen gas mixture ratio, treatment temperature, and electrical discharge parameters during processing. Gas nitriding relies on ammonia dissociation rates from 15% to 30% to regulate nitrogen supply, producing less consistent compound layer control across complex component geometries. Plasma nitriding operates at lower temperatures from 350°C to 570°C, reducing thermal distortion on precision components requiring dimensional tolerances within 0.025 mm after treatment. The localized surface activation in plasma nitriding allows selective hardening of specific surface areas without masking, reducing preparation time compared to gas nitriding processes that require physical masking for selective treatment. What Materials Are Suitable for Nitriding? The materials that are suitable for nitriding are listed below. Alloy steels are commonly used in nitriding because chromium, aluminum, and molybdenum present in the steel matrix react readily with diffused nitrogen atoms to form hard nitride compounds throughout the case layer. The nitride-forming alloying elements produce dense nitride distributions that raise surface hardness values from 650 HV to 900 HV, exceeding the hardness achievable in plain carbon steels under identical nitriding conditions. Chromium content from 0.7% to 1.1 % in alloy steel grades (4140, 4340) produces consistent chromium nitride (CrN) distributions, delivering reliable case depths from 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm across treated components. Molybdenum content from 0.15% to 0.4% contributes additional nitride formation, raising core toughness and reducing brittleness within the hardened case layer. Aluminum content from 0.85% to 1.5% produces the highest nitride density among common alloying elements, generating surface hardness values of 1,200 HV in dedicated nitriding grades. The combination of multiple nitride-forming elements in Alloy Steels makes them the most consistently responsive material class for industrial nitriding applications. Can Plain Carbon Steels Be Nitrided Effectively? No, plain carbon steels cannot be nitrided effectively. The absence of nitride-forming alloying elements (aluminum, chromium, molybdenum) prevents dense nitride distributions from developing within the case layer. Nitrogen diffuses into the steel matrix but reacts with iron, forming iron nitrides (Fe2N, Fe3N, Fe4N) that carry hardness values from 250 HV to 400 HV, significantly lower than the 650 HV to 1,200 HV achieved in alloy steel grades. The iron nitride compounds produce a brittle compound layer that fractures under cyclic loading and abrasive contact conditions, limiting functional performance across precision manufacturing environments. Alloy steel grades with chromium, aluminum, and molybdenum content remain the preferred material selection for nitriding applications requiring consistent surface hardness and wear resistance, compared to Plain Carbon Steels . What Mechanical Properties Change During Nitriding? The mechanical properties that change during nitriding are listed below. Surface hardness values increase from a pre-treatment range of 200 HV to 350 HV to 650 HV to 1,200 HV, depending on the base material composition and treatment parameters. Improved Wear Resistance : The hardened nitride case layer resists abrasive and adhesive wear under contact loading conditions, extending component service life across high-load applications. Improved Fatigue Strength : Nitriding introduces compressive residual stresses into the surface layer, raising the fatigue strength of treated components by 20% to 40% compared to untreated base material. Better Corrosion Resistance : Nitrided stainless steel and aluminum-bearing alloy grades develop a dense nitride surface layer that reduces oxidation and corrosion rates in moderate chemical environments. Nitriding improves fatigue resistance by introducing compressive residual stresses into the surface layer during nitrogen diffusion and nitride formation. The compressive stress layer counteracts tensile fatigue stresses generated at the component surface under cyclic loading, delaying crack initiation at stress concentration points (notches, fillets, surface defects). What Equipment Is Used in Nitriding? The equipment that is used in nitriding is listed below. Higher dissociation rates above 85% reduce nitrogen activity at the surface, accelerating case depth development while lowering surface hardness values across treated components. How Does Nitriding Compare to Carburizing? Ammonia dissociation rates falling below 15% increase nitrogen concentration at the surface, accelerating compound layer growth beyond the functional thickness range. A compound layer exceeding 0.05 mm demonstrates brittleness under cyclic loading, initiating surface cracks that propagate into the diffusion zone beneath the hardened case. Overnitriding at temperatures below 480°C reduces nitrogen diffusion depth, concentrating nitride formation at the immediate surface and producing a shallow, brittle case layer with reduced fatigue resistance. Post-nitriding compound layer thickness measurements using metallographic cross-sections confirm whether the white layer remains within the acceptable range from 0.01 mm to 0.03 mm across precision components.
