events.after: Resources / Materials / Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Sulfur (S): Formula, Element and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 24 min read Published June 10, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Sulfur (S) is a bright yellow, nonmetallic chemical element with the atomic number 16 and the chemical symbol S, occurring abundantly in nature as elemental deposits near volcanic regions and as sulfide and sulfate minerals throughout Earth's crust. Sulfur (S) ranks among the most industrially significant nonmetals, serving as the foundational raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), the most widely produced industrial chemical globally, with annual production exceeding 270 million metric tons. The element's chemical reactivity, low cost, and availability drive its application across fertilizer manufacturing, rubber vulcanization, petroleum refining, pharmaceuticals, and surface treatment processes. Sulfur connects to metal processing through sulfuric acid anodizing, where H₂SO₄ acts as the electrolyte to form protective oxide layers on aluminum surfaces, improving corrosion and wear resistance. In metallurgy, controlled sulfur additions to steel and nickel alloys form manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that improve machinability by promoting chip breakage during cutting operations, a property exploited in free-machining grades (12L14 steel, Monel 405). Sulfur's interactions with steel types and grades, nickel alloys, and surface treatment chemistry establish it as a chemically active element with consequences across manufacturing, agriculture, energy, and materials engineering. What Is Sulfur (S)? Sulfur (S) is a chemical element found in minerals and industrial materials, classified as a nonmetal with atomic number 16, atomic mass 32.06 u, and the chemical symbol S. In its elemental form, sulfur is a bright yellow, brittle solid at room temperature, odorless when pure but producing the characteristic pungent smell of hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) or sulfur dioxide (SO₂) when burned or reduced. Sulfur ranks as the 10th most abundant element in the universe and the 5th most abundant element on Earth by mass, occurring in volcanic deposits, evaporite minerals (gypsum, anhydrite), and sulfide ores (pyrite, galena, cinnabar). The element is the starting material for sulfuric acid production, the world's most consumed industrial chemical. Sulfur participates in the biological amino acids cysteine and methionine, making it an essential element for all living organisms. In industrial contexts, sulfur drives chemical manufacturing, rubber processing, fertilizer production, and metallurgical applications across dozens of sectors. The smell of sulfur, in its pure elemental form, is essentially odorless at room temperature. The strong, unpleasant smell commonly associated with sulfur comes from sulfur compounds, primarily hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), which produces an odor resembling rotten eggs at concentrations as low as 0.5 parts per billion (ppb), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂), which emits a sharp, pungent, choking odor at concentrations above 1 ppm. What Is the Chemical Formula of Sulfur (S)? The chemical formula of Sulfur is represented by the symbol S as a single element, but in its most stable naturally occurring molecular form, it exists as S₈, a crown-shaped ring of eight covalently bonded sulfur atoms. The S₈ molecule, known as cyclooctasulfur or orthorhombic sulfur, is the thermodynamically stable allotrope of sulfur at room temperature and standard pressure. Each sulfur atom in the S₈ ring forms two covalent bonds with adjacent sulfur atoms, completing its valence shell without forming double bonds in the ring structure. Sulfur also exists in other allotropic forms: S₆ (rhombohedral sulfur), S₁₂, and polymeric sulfur (plastic sulfur), a chain-like amorphous form produced by quenching molten sulfur in cold water. In chemical compounds, sulfur appears in formulas including H₂SO₄ (sulfuric acid), H₂S (hydrogen sulfide), SO₂ (sulfur dioxide), and Na₂SO₄ (sodium sulfate), each reflecting sulfur's variable oxidation states from -2 to +6. What Is Sulfur (S) as a Chemical Element? Sulfur is a nonmetallic chemical element in Group 16 (chalcogens) of the periodic table, Period 3, with the atomic number 16 and the standard atomic weight of 32.06 u. The element has an electronegativity of 2.58 on the Pauling scale, a value reflecting its moderate tendency to attract electrons in covalent bonds, placing it below oxygen (3.44) and above carbon (2.55). Sulfur has four naturally occurring stable isotopes: sulfur-32 (94.93%), sulfur-33 (0.76%), sulfur-34 (4.29%), and sulfur-36 (0.02%), with sulfur-32 dominating natural abundance. The electron configuration of sulfur is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴, providing six valence electrons that drive its chemical bonding in compounds ranging from sulfides (-2 oxidation state) to sulfates (+6 oxidation state). Sulfur melts at 115.2°C and boils at 444.6°C, properties that make it processable at relatively low temperatures compared to metals, supporting its use in chemical manufacturing and vulcanization processes. Is Sulfur a Metal or Nonmetal? Sulfur is a nonmetal, and its physical and chemical properties confirm the classification across every relevant criterion. At room temperature, sulfur is a brittle, yellow solid that fractures when struck, lacking the malleability and ductility characteristic of metals. Sulfur's electrical conductivity is extremely low at approximately 10⁻¹⁵ S/m, making it an electrical insulator rather than a conductor. Thermal conductivity measures 0.205 W/(m·K), far below the values of metals (iron: 80 W/(m·K), copper: 400 W/(m·K)). Sulfur does not exhibit metallic luster; its surface is dull and matte yellow. Chemically, sulfur gains electrons (acts as an oxidizing agent) instead of donating them, a behavior opposite to metals. The combination of brittleness, non-conductivity, low thermal conductivity, and electron-gaining behavior classifies sulfur unambiguously as a nonmetal. How Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Connected to Sulfur Chemistry? Sulfuric acid anodizing is connected to sulfur-based compounds, specifically sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), as the electrolyte solution that drives the electrochemical formation of a protective aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer on aluminum surfaces, connecting sulfur chemistry directly to metal surface engineering. In the anodizing process, aluminum parts are immersed in a sulfuric acid bath with concentrations from 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ by weight, at temperatures from 18°C to 22°C, and a direct current is applied at voltage levels from 12 V to 21 V. The sulfuric acid provides the ionic conductivity needed to sustain the electrochemical reaction, where oxygen ions generated at the anode react with the aluminum surface to grow a porous Al₂O₃ film from 5 µm to 25 µm thick. Sulfur incorporates into the oxide film as sulfate ions, typically comprising 12% to 15% of the layer by weight, and is the chemically active component of the electrolyte that governs film growth rate, porosity, and thickness. Xometry's surface finishing services include sulfuric acid anodizing for aluminum components requiring improved corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and decorative finish quality. How Is Sulfuric Acid Used in Anodizing Processes? Sulfuric acid is used in anodizing processes as the primary electrolyte in Type II (standard) and Type III (hard coat), providing the ionic medium through which electrical current flows and aluminum oxide grows on the workpiece surface. A 15% to 20% H₂SO₄ solution at 18°C to 22°C and 12 V to 21 V produces an oxide layer from 5 µm to 25 µm thick with moderate porosity in Type II anodizing, suitable for dyeing and corrosion protection in architectural and consumer applications. Higher H₂SO₄ concentrations (up to 25%) combined with lower temperatures (0°C to 5°C) and higher voltages (25 V to 100 V) produce denser oxide layers from 25 µm to 100 µm thick in Type III hard coat anodizing, with hardness from 400 HV to 600 HV, suitable for wear-resistant military, aerospace, and industrial components. The sulfuric acid electrolyte simultaneously drives oxide growth at the barrier layer and partially dissolves the outer porous layer, controlling the equilibrium between oxide formation and dissolution that determines final film thickness and structure. Is Sulfuric Acid Anodizing Used to Improve Metal Corrosion Resistance? Yes, sulfuric acid anodizing is used to improve metal corrosion resistance by converting the aluminum surface into a thick, stable aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃) layer that acts as a physical barrier preventing moisture, oxygen, and corrosive agents from reaching the underlying metal. The anodized Al₂O₃ layer produced in sulfuric acid electrolyte is integral to the aluminum surface, growing both inward and outward from the original metal surface, and does not peel or delaminate like applied coatings. Salt spray testing (ASTM B117) confirms that Type II anodized aluminum withstands 336 hours to 500 hours of salt fog without corrosion failure, while Type III hard coat anodized surfaces exceed 1,000 hours. Sealing the anodized layer in hot water (96°C to 100°C) or nickel acetate solution closes the pores, further improving corrosion resistance by preventing electrolyte penetration into the oxide structure. How Does Sulfur Interact With Steel Types and Grades? Sulfur interacts with steel types and grades through its role as an impurity that affects the steel’s properties. Sulfur is added in controlled amounts to specific steel grades to improve machinability through the formation of manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions, soft non-metallic particles that act as internal lubricants and chip breakers during cutting operations, reducing tool wear and improving surface finish. Sulfur content ranges from 0.08% to 0.35% by weight in free-machining steels, well above the residual sulfur levels below 0.05% maintained in structural and high-strength steel grades. MnS inclusions form when manganese reacts with sulfur during solidification, precipitating as elongated particles oriented in the rolling direction of the steel bar or plate. The elongated MnS particles disrupt the continuity of the steel matrix in the machining zone, promoting chip breakage and reducing cutting forces by 15% to 30% compared to equivalent low-sulfur grades. Excess sulfur above the specified range reduces transverse toughness, ductility, and weldability, requiring careful composition control in free-machining steel types and grades . How Does Sulfur Affect 4140 Alloy Steel? Sulfur affects 4140 alloy steel, improving machinability by forming MnS inclusions that act as chip breakers during turning, milling, and drilling operations, reducing cutting forces and extending tool life in high-volume machining environments. Standard 4140 steel (AISI/SAE specification) contains sulfur as a residual element limited to a maximum of 0.040% by weight, a level low enough to preserve toughness, fatigue resistance, and weldability while permitting minor machinability benefits. Free-machining variants of 4140 incorporate sulfur from 0.08% to 0.13%, producing a measurable increase in machinability rating from approximately 55% to 70% of the AISI 1212 baseline. The tradeoff of elevated sulfur in 4140 is a reduction in Charpy impact toughness in the transverse direction, where MnS inclusions act as crack initiation sites. Xometry's CNC machining services process 4140 alloy steel in standard and free-machining variants, with material selection guided by the balance of machinability to the mechanical performance required for each component. How Does Sulfur Affect 1020 Carbon Steel? Sulfur affects 1020 carbon steel, improving machinability through MnS inclusion formation, with standard 1020 (AISI/SAE) containing sulfur limited to a maximum of 0.050% and free-machining 1215 steel (a sulfur-enhanced low-carbon grade) containing 0.26% to 0.35% sulfur for maximum cutting efficiency. The machinability rating of low-carbon steel increases significantly; 12L14 (leaded, sulfurized) reaches a machinability rating of 170% relative to the AISI 1212 baseline at sulfur levels from 0.26% to 0.35%, while 1215 (sulfurized, non-leaded) achieves 136%. The MnS inclusions in sulfurized 1020-class steels reduce cutting tool temperature by acting as a solid lubricant at the tool-chip interface, lowering crater wear rates on carbide and high-speed steel tooling. Elevated sulfur in low-carbon grades reduces weldability and cold-forming performance, limiting free-machining sulfurized steels to machined-only applications where subsequent welding or forming is not required, especially in 1020 carbon steel . How Does Sulfur Affect Stainless Steel? Sulfur affects stainless steel, improving machinability but reducing corrosion resistance, requiring precise composition control to balance cutting performance against the corrosion protection that defines the material's primary function. Standard austenitic grades (304, 316) limit sulfur to a maximum of 0.030% to preserve the integrity of the passive Cr₂O₃ film; MnS inclusions at higher sulfur levels act as initiation sites for pitting corrosion in chloride environments, where sulfide inclusions dissolve preferentially and create corrosion pits in the surrounding matrix. Grade 303 stainless steel is the primary free-machining austenitic variant, containing 0.15% minimum sulfur, a level that dramatically improves machinability (approximately 78% of the AISI 1212 baseline, versus 45% for 304) at the cost of reduced pitting and crevice corrosion resistance relative to 304. The balance from machinability to corrosion resistance in sulfur-controlled stainless steel grades is governed by the intended service environment and the severity of corrosive exposure. Does Sulfur Improve Machinability in Different Steel Grades? Yes, sulfur improves machinability in different steel grades by forming manganese sulfide (MnS) inclusions that reduce cutting forces, promote chip breakage, and decrease tool wear during turning, milling, drilling, and threading operations. The machinability improvement is quantified by the AISI machinability rating system, where 1212 steel (0.70% to 1.00% Mn, 0.16% to 0.23% S ) serves as the 100% baseline. Grades with increasing sulfur content show proportional machinability gains: 1215 (0.26% to 0.35% S) achieves 136%, 12L14 (sulfur plus lead) reaches 170%, and 303 stainless (0.15% min S) achieves 78% versus 304's 45%. The machinability benefit of sulfur applies across low-carbon, medium-carbon, alloy, and stainless steel categories, making sulfur the most cost-effective machinability additive in steel composition design. What Is the Role of Sulfur in Nickel Alloys? The role of Sulfur in nickel alloys is added in controlled amounts to specific free-machining grades to improve machinability through sulfide inclusion formation, while in standard structural nickel alloys, sulfur is treated as a harmful impurity limited to trace levels below 0.010% due to its severe embrittling effect on nickel at elevated temperatures. Nickel is highly susceptible to sulfur embrittlement; sulfur forms nickel sulfide (Ni₃S₂) at grain boundaries in nickel-rich alloys, a compound that melts at 637°C and creates liquid-phase grain boundary films that cause hot cracking during welding and hot working at temperatures above 600°C. Sulfur is balanced against manganese content to promote MnS formation rather than Ni₃S₂ in free-machining nickel alloy grades, directing sulfur into benign nickel-copper sulfide inclusions that aid chip breakage without causing grain boundary embrittlement. Xometry's manufacturing network processes nickel alloys across free-machining and standard grades, with sulfur content specified according to the mechanical and machinability requirements of each application. How Is Sulfur Related to Monel 405? Sulfur is related to Monel 405 at levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight to improve machinability, distinguishing grade 405 from Monel 400, which contains residual sulfur below 0.024% and offers superior corrosion resistance but lower machinability. Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy (approximately 63% to 70% Ni, 28% to 34% Cu) where the sulfur addition promotes sulfide inclusion formation that aids chip formation during turning, drilling, and threading on automatic screw machines. The controlled sulfur content in Monel 405 raises its machinability rating to approximately 30% of the AISI 1212 baseline, compared to Monel 400's 22%, a meaningful improvement for high-volume machined parts. Sulfur content in Monel 405 is kept within the 0.025% to 0.060% range to ensure nickel-copper sulfide inclusions form preferentially over nickel sulfides, avoiding grain boundary embrittlement while delivering the machinability benefit that defines the grade. How Is Sulfur Related to Post Transition Metal Alloys? Sulfur in post-transition metal alloys (alloys based on elements including aluminum, lead, tin, bismuth, and indium) acts as an impurity or a deliberate additive that influences machinability and mechanical properties, depending on the specific alloy system and sulfur concentration. In aluminum alloys, sulfur is not a common additive; it appears as trace contamination at levels below 0.001%, with negligible effect on mechanical properties at the concentrations encountered in standard production. Sulfur interacts with lead and tin to form sulfide phases that influence solidification microstructure and casting surface quality in lead-based free-machining alloys and tin-bronze casting alloys. The effects of sulfur in post-transition metal alloys are alloy-system specific, requiring composition-dependent assessment rather than a universal characterization, as sulfur's role shifts from beneficial machinability additive to harmful impurity depending on the base metal's affinity for sulfide formation. Is Monel 405 a Nickel-Copper Alloy That Contains Controlled Sulfur Levels? Yes, Monel 405 is a nickel-copper alloy that contains controlled sulfur levels from 0.025% to 0.060% by weight, a compositional feature that defines the grade's identity as the free-machining variant of the Monel 400 family. The base composition of Monel 405 is nickel from 63% to 70% and copper from 28% to 34%, with the sulfur addition as the primary differentiating variable from Monel 400. Controlled sulfur in Monel 405 produces sulfide inclusions that break chips during automatic screw machine operations, enabling the manufacture of fittings, valve stems, and precision fasteners at production rates impractical with standard Monel 400. The sulfur range of 0.025% to 0.060% is tightly specified in ASTM B164 (standard specification for Monel rod, bar, and wire) to ensure consistent machinability without compromising corrosion resistance beyond acceptable limits for moderate service environments, making it suitable for applications where machinability is essential without sacrificing the key properties of Monel 405 . What Are the Uses of Sulfur? The uses of Sulfur are listed below. Production of Sulfuric Acid : Sulfur is the primary raw material for sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) synthesis via the Contact process, with over 270 million metric tons of H₂SO₄ produced globally each year. Fertilizer Manufacturing : Sulfur and sulfuric acid are used to produce ammonium sulfate, superphosphate, and other sulfur-containing fertilizers that supply essential nutrients to crops. Rubber Vulcanization : Sulfur crosslinks polymer chains in natural and synthetic rubber during vulcanization, converting soft, tacky rubber into durable, elastic material with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 30 MPa. Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder : Sulfur serves as a fuel component in black powder (10% sulfur) and as an ignition component in match heads and pyrotechnic compositions. Pesticides and Fungicides : Elemental sulfur and sulfur compounds are applied as fungicides and acaricides in agriculture, effective against powdery mildew, rust, and spider mites at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 5 kg/ha. Pharmaceuticals and Medicines : Sulfur compounds appear in antibiotics (sulfonamides), antifungal treatments (selenium sulfide), and topical acne medications containing sulfur from 3% to 10% concentration. Petroleum Refining : Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) removes sulfur compounds from crude oil fractions, producing recovered elemental sulfur as a byproduct while reducing sulfur in fuels to below 10 ppm to meet emission standards. Detergents and Chemical Products : Sulfonation reactions using SO₃ or H₂SO₄ produce sulfonate surfactants (linear alkylbenzene sulfonate, sodium lauryl sulfate) that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. "It is easy to forget that a clean CAD model still has to face the messy realities of metallurgy on the shop floor. While adding sulfur makes a steel grade incredibly efficient to machine, it can quietly compromise the part's weldability or toughness. Solid design for manufacturing always looks past the screen to balance structural performance with actual machining costs." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 1. Sulfur Used for Production of Sulfuric Acid Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) production is the largest single use of sulfur globally, consuming approximately 90% of elemental sulfur produced each year, with global H₂SO₄ output exceeding 270 million metric tons annually. The Contact process converts elemental sulfur into sulfuric acid through three sequential reactions: combustion of sulfur to sulfur dioxide (S + O₂ → SO₂), catalytic oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ over vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) catalyst at temperatures from 400°C to 600°C (2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃), and absorption of SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to produce oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is then diluted with water to the target acid concentration. The double absorption Contact process achieves SO₂ conversion efficiencies above 99.7%, minimizing atmospheric SO₂ emissions while maximizing acid yield. Sulfuric acid produced from sulfur serves as the feedstock for fertilizer manufacturing (phosphoric acid, ammonium sulfate), petroleum refining (alkylation), metal processing (pickling, anodizing), battery acid (lead-acid batteries), and dozens of chemical synthesis pathways across nearly every industrial sector. 2. Sulfur Used for Fertilizer Manufacturing Sulfur and sulfuric acid are fundamental to fertilizer manufacturing, supplying both the sulfur nutrient required by plants and the acidifying agent needed to convert phosphate rock into water-soluble plant-available phosphate fertilizers. Superphosphate fertilizer is produced by reacting phosphate rock (Ca₃(PO₄)₂) with sulfuric acid to produce calcium dihydrogen phosphate (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂) and calcium sulfate (gypsum), with single superphosphate containing approximately 20% P₂O₅ and triple superphosphate reaching 44% to 48% P₂O₅. Ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄) fertilizer, containing 21% nitrogen and 24% sulfur, is produced from sulfuric acid and ammonia and provides both macronutrients in a single product. Elemental sulfur applied directly to alkaline soils acidifies the root zone through bacterial oxidation to H₂SO₄ (by Thiobacillus bacteria), improving nutrient availability in high-pH soils. Global sulfur consumption in fertilizer production exceeds 50 million metric tons annually, reflecting agriculture's dependence on sulfur chemistry to maintain crop yields. Sulfur Used for Rubber Vulcanization Sulfur vulcanization converts natural rubber (polyisoprene) and synthetic rubbers (SBR, NBR, EPDM) from soft, thermoplastic materials into durable, elastic solids by forming covalent sulfur crosslinks from 1 to 8 sulfur atoms long, connecting adjacent polymer chains. Charles Goodyear discovered sulfur vulcanization in 1839, observing that heating rubber with sulfur at temperatures from 140°C to 180°C produced a material with dramatically improved mechanical properties, temperature stability, and resistance to solvent swelling. Sulfur loading in rubber compounds ranges from 0.5 parts per hundred rubber (phr) for efficient vulcanization systems to 30 phr to 50 phr for hard rubber (ebonite), which is fully crosslinked and rigid. Vulcanized rubber with 1 phr to 3 phr sulfur produces soft elastic products (gloves, balloons, foam) with tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa and elongation at break from 500% to 800%. Tire compounds use sulfur from 1.5 phr to 3.5 phr combined with accelerators (CBS, MBT) and activators (zinc oxide, stearic acid) to achieve the crosslink density required for tread wear, flex fatigue resistance, and heat buildup control in service. 4. Sulfur Used for Matches, Fireworks, and Gunpowder Sulfur serves as a fuel and combustion-modifier component in pyrotechnic compositions, contributing to ignition sensitivity, burn rate, and energy output in matches, fireworks, and black powder. Black powder (gunpowder) contains approximately 75% potassium nitrate (KNO₃), 15% charcoal, and 10% sulfur by weight; sulfur lowers the ignition temperature of the mixture, acts as a fuel, and reacts with potassium nitrate to produce potassium sulfide and release energy at a controlled rate suitable for propellant and pyrotechnic applications. Match heads in strike-anywhere matches contain sulfur compounds (antimony trisulfide, Sb₂S₃) combined with oxidizers and friction-sensitive materials that ignite at temperatures from 180°C to 230°C. In fireworks compositions, sulfur is incorporated into lift charges, burst charges, and color-producing stars, where its role as a reducing fuel complements oxidizers like potassium perchlorate (KClO₄) and potassium nitrate to sustain combustion at temperatures from 1,500°C to 2,000°C, producing the visual and auditory effects of aerial pyrotechnics. 5. Sulfur Used for Pesticides and Fungicides Elemental sulfur is one of the oldest and most widely used agricultural pesticides, applied as a fungicide, acaricide (miticide), and insecticide against a broad range of plant pathogens and arthropod pests at application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, depending on crop and pest pressure. Sulfur controls fungal diseases, including powdery mildew (Erysiphe spp.), rust (Puccinia spp.), and scab (Venturia inaequalis) on grapes, stone fruits, and vegetables through direct contact toxicity, where sulfur vapor at the leaf surface inhibits fungal spore germination and disrupts cellular respiration in the pathogen. Wettable sulfur and sulfur dust formulations with particle sizes from 3 µm to 10 µm provide maximum surface coverage and fungicidal activity on crop foliage. Lime sulfur (calcium polysulfide, CaS₅) is a liquid formulation used as a dormant spray on fruit trees, controlling overwintering fungal inoculum and scale insects at dilutions from 1:10 to 1:50 in water. Sulfur-based pesticides are approved for organic agriculture under USDA National Organic Program (NOP) standards, making sulfur one of the few broad-spectrum pest control agents compatible with certified organic production systems. 6. Sulfur Used for Pharmaceuticals and Medicines Sulfur and sulfur-containing compounds appear across a wide range of pharmaceutical applications, from topical dermatological treatments to systemic antibiotics, reflecting sulfur's biological reactivity and its presence in amino acids essential to protein structure. Elemental sulfur in concentrations from 3% to 10% is used in topical acne treatments, where it acts as a keratolytic agent that breaks down excess keratin, reduces sebaceous gland activity, and exhibits mild antibacterial properties against Cutibacterium acnes. Sulfonamide antibiotics (sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine) contain a sulfonamide group (-SO₂-NH₂) that inhibits bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis in susceptible bacteria at minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) from 1 µg/mL to 64 µg/mL. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, (CH₃)₂SO) is used as a pharmaceutical carrier and anti-inflammatory agent, with FDA approval for treatment of interstitial cystitis at a 50% concentration instilled directly into the bladder. Selenium sulfide (SeS₂), a sulfur-containing compound, is the active ingredient in medicated shampoos for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis at concentrations from 1% to 2.5%. Sulfur Used for Petroleum Refining Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) is the primary petroleum refining process that removes sulfur-containing compounds from crude oil fractions, converting organosulfur compounds (thiophenes, benzothiophenes, mercaptans) to hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and sulfur-free hydrocarbons over cobalt-molybdenum or nickel-molybdenum catalysts at temperatures from 300°C to 400°C and hydrogen pressures from 3 MPa to 13 MPa. The recovered H₂S is converted to elemental sulfur via the Claus process, making petroleum refining the world's largest single source of recovered elemental sulfur, accounting for approximately 80% of global sulfur supply. Ultra-low sulfur diesel (ULSD) regulations in the United States and European Union require sulfur content below 15 ppm and 10 ppm, respectively, driving extensive HDS capacity in modern refineries. The removal of sulfur from petroleum products reduces SO₂ emissions from combustion engines, protects catalytic converters from sulfur poisoning, and meets air quality standards that limit atmospheric SO₂ concentrations to protect human health and reduce acid rain formation. 8. Sulfur Used for Detergents and Chemical Products Sulfonation reactions using sulfur trioxide (SO₃) or oleum (fuming sulfuric acid) introduce sulfonate groups (-SO₃H) into organic molecules, producing surfactants that form the active cleaning agents in laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids, shampoos, and industrial cleaners. Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS), produced by sulfonating linear alkylbenzene with SO₃ at temperatures from 40°C to 60°C, is the most widely produced surfactant globally, with annual production exceeding 3 million metric tons. Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), produced by reacting lauryl alcohol with SO₃ or chlorosulfuric acid, is the primary surfactant in shampoos, toothpastes, and personal care products at concentrations from 5% to 30%. Sulfosuccinate surfactants (dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, DOSS) are used as wetting agents and emulsifiers in pharmaceutical formulations, food processing, and industrial applications. The sulfonate group's hydrophilic character (water-attracting) combined with the hydrophobic carbon chain of the parent molecule creates the amphiphilic structure responsible for surfactant cleaning action, making sulfur chemistry the foundation of the global detergent industry. What Are the Advantages of Using Sulfur? The advantages of using Sulfur are listed below. Abundant and Low Cost : Sulfur is among the most abundant elements on Earth and is recovered as a byproduct of petroleum refining and natural gas processing, making it one of the lowest-cost industrial raw materials at commodity prices from [$30 to $150] per metric ton depending on market conditions. Versatile Chemical Reactivity : Sulfur's ability to adopt oxidation states from -2 to +6 enables its use across an exceptionally wide range of chemical reactions, from reduction in rubber vulcanization to oxidation in sulfuric acid production, giving it unmatched chemical versatility among nonmetals. Effective Agricultural Nutrient : Sulfur is an essential macronutrient for plant growth, required for the synthesis of amino acids (cysteine, methionine) and chlorophyll. Sulfur-deficient soils treated with elemental sulfur or sulfate fertilizers show crop yield improvements from 10% to 40%, depending on deficiency severity and crop type. Machinability Enhancement in Metals : Controlled sulfur additions from 0.08% to 0.35% in free-machining steel grades reduce cutting forces by 15% to 30% and extend tool life significantly, lowering manufacturing costs in high-volume machining operations without expensive alloying additions. Environmentally Recoverable : Sulfur recovered from petroleum refining and natural gas sweetening operations converts a potential atmospheric pollutant (H₂S, SO₂) into a commercially valuable material, reducing environmental sulfur emissions while supplying industrial demand without additional mining. Effective Fungicidal Action : Elemental sulfur controls a broad spectrum of fungal diseases and mites in agriculture at low application rates from 1 kg/ha to 10 kg/ha, with low mammalian toxicity (oral LD₅₀ greater than 3,000 mg/kg in rats) and approval for organic farming, making it one of the safest broad-spectrum crop protection agents available. High Energy Output in Combustion : Sulfur combustion releases approximately 9.16 MJ/kg, a useful energy density for pyrotechnic and combustion applications in black powder, fireworks, and certain industrial heating processes where sulfur's low cost and predictable burn characteristics are advantageous. Essential Role in Biochemistry : Sulfur's presence in amino acids (cysteine, methionine), vitamins (biotin, thiamine), and coenzymes (coenzyme A) makes sulfur compounds indispensable in pharmaceutical synthesis, nutritional supplementation, and biotechnology applications where biologically active sulfur-containing molecules are produced at a commercial scale. events.before: Resources / Materials / Synthetic Rubber: Material and Examples Synthetic Rubber: Material and Examples Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 26 min read Published June 22, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Synthetic rubber is a manufactured elastomer produced through the chemical polymerization of petroleum-derived monomers, engineered to replicate and exceed the mechanical properties of natural rubber. Synthetic rubber originates from petrochemical feedstocks processed into reactive monomers, including styrene, butadiene, isoprene, chloroprene, and acrylonitrile, which form long-chain elastomeric polymers. Synthetic rubber is produced through emulsion, solution, or gas-phase, followed by compounding and vulcanization. Primary types include Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR), Neoprene, Nitrile Rubber (NBR), Butyl Rubber (IIR), EPDM, Silicone Rubber, and Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR), each engineered for specific performance requirements. Examples span tires, seals, gaskets, hoses, gloves, and industrial conveyor systems across automotive, aerospace, medical, and construction industries. What Is Synthetic Rubber? Synthetic rubber is an artificially manufactured elastomer produced through the chemical polymerization of petroleum-derived monomers, designed to replicate the elastic and resilient properties of natural rubber while offering enhanced resistance to heat, chemicals, UV radiation, and mechanical stress. The material returns to its original shape after deformation, with elongation at break values ranging from 100% to over 800% depending on polymer type. Synthetic rubber accounts for approximately 60% to 65% of total global rubber consumption, with production reaching approximately 15 million metric tons annually. The material is formulated from monomers, including butadiene, styrene, isoprene, chloroprene, and ethylene, bonded into polymer chains through controlled industrial processes. Products range from automotive tires and industrial seals to medical gloves and construction membranes, with hardness measurable on the Shore A scale from 20 to 90. How Is Synthetic Rubber Defined in Simple Terms? Synthetic rubber is a man-made elastic material produced from petroleum-derived chemicals, engineered to stretch, compress, and return to its original shape under repeated mechanical stress. The term "synthetic" indicates the material does not originate from the rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) but from industrial chemical processes that construct its polymer structure entirely from petrochemical inputs. Synthetic rubber performs like natural rubber but is manufactured with greater consistency and adjusted chemically to operate in conditions natural rubber cannot tolerate, including temperatures below -50°C or above 200°C, prolonged oil immersion, and continuous UV exposure. Hardness is measured on the Shore A durometer scale from 20 (very soft) to 90 (hard rubber), allowing precise flexibility specification for any application from surgical gloves to industrial conveyor belts. Is Synthetic Rubber Considered a Synthetic Polymer? Synthetic rubber is considered a synthetic polymer. Its molecular structure consists of long-chain repeating monomer units chemically bonded through polymerization reactions conducted entirely through industrial processes. Every commercially produced synthetic rubber type, including SBR, NBR, and EPDM, qualifies as a synthetic polymer under standard polymer chemistry definitions. Polymer chains in synthetic rubber are constructed from petroleum-derived monomers with molecular weights per repeat unit ranging from 54 g/mol (butadiene) to 88.5 g/mol (chloroprene). The resulting polymer reaches a molecular weight of 100,000 to over 1,000,000 g/mol, producing the elastic, high-elongation properties characteristic of rubber. Crosslinking during vulcanization creates a three-dimensional network that defines the final mechanical performance. Comprehensive material classifications are covered under synthetic polymers. Where Does Synthetic Rubber Come From? Synthetic rubber originates from the petrochemical industry, where crude oil and natural gas are refined and cracked into reactive monomers that serve as building blocks for elastomeric polymer synthesis. Commercial production began in Germany during World War I and expanded significantly during World War II with mass production of GR-S (Government Rubber-Styrene), the precursor to modern SBR. Major production centers are located in China, the United States, Russia, Japan, and Germany, with China holding the largest global output share. The primary feedstock, naphtha, is produced during crude oil distillation at 30°C to 200°C and further processed through steam cracking at 750°C to 900°C to yield butadiene, ethylene, propylene, and benzene for rubber polymerization. What Are the Main Sources of Synthetic Rubber? The main sources of synthetic rubber are listed below. Crude Oil (Naphtha Fraction): Naphtha steam-cracked at 750°C to 900°C yields butadiene, styrene, isoprene, and ethylene, as well as benzene, used to synthesize styrene, the primary monomers for SBR, polybutadiene, polyisoprene, and EPDM production. Naphtha-derived monomers supply the majority of global synthetic rubber feedstock. Natural Gas Processing: Ethane and propane fractions cracked from natural gas produce ethylene and propylene, monomers used in EPDM synthesis Coal Tar (Historical Source) : Coal tar distillation historically yielded benzene and toluene for early synthetic rubber production. Petroleum sources have since replaced coal-derived feedstocks in commercial manufacturing. Bio-based Feedstocks (Emerging Source) : Fermentation of sugarcane or corn starch generates bio-based butadiene and isoprene for bio-SBR and bio-polyisoprene production. Bio-based synthetic rubber currently represents less than 5% of total global output but is growing as sustainability targets increase across automotive sectors. Acetylene (Historical Source) : Acetylene-based routes were used in early chloroprene production but have been replaced by butadiene-based processes in modern neoprene manufacturing. Does Synthetic Rubber Come From Petroleum Based Materials? Synthetic rubber comes predominantly from petroleum-based materials. Crude oil and natural gas supply the chemical monomers polymerized into synthetic rubber at an industrial scale, with approximately 95% or more of global production relying on petroleum-derived monomers, including butadiene, styrene, isoprene, ethylene, propylene, and acrylonitrile. Crude oil is refined through fractional distillation to yield naphtha, which is steam-cracked to produce the reactive monomers entering rubber polymerization reactors. The price of synthetic rubber is consequently sensitive to crude oil fluctuations: a 10% increase in crude oil prices typically translates to a 5% to 8% increase in synthetic rubber raw material costs within 30 to 90 days. Petroleum's role as the dominant feedstock represents a supply scale advantage and a vulnerability during oil price volatility. What Is Synthetic Rubber Made Of? Synthetic rubber is made of polymerized chemical monomers derived from petroleum refining, formulated with vulcanizing agents, fillers, plasticizers, and antioxidants to produce the final compounded elastomer. The specific monomer composition determines polymer type and performance, while compounding additives govern processing behavior and end-use properties. Core monomers include butadiene (C₄H₆), styrene (C₈H₈), isoprene (C₅H₈), chloroprene (C₄H₅Cl), acrylonitrile (C₃H₃N), ethylene (C₂H₄), and propylene (C₃H₆). Butadiene is the most widely consumed monomer, accounting for approximately 60% to 70% of total monomer usage across rubber types. Compounding additives include sulfur at 1% to 5% by weight (vulcanizing agent), carbon black at 20% to 50% by weight (reinforcing filler), zinc oxide at 3% to 5% by weight (vulcanization activator), processing oils at 5% to 30% by weight (plasticizer), and antioxidants at 0.5% to 2% by weight. Which Materials Are Used in Synthetic Rubber Production? The materials that are used in synthetic rubber production are listed below. Butadiene (C₄H₆) : The primary monomer in SBR, polybutadiene, and NBR, produced from naphtha steam cracking. Global butadiene production exceeds 12 million metric tons annually, with approximately 65% directed to synthetic rubber manufacturing. Styrene (C₈H₈) : A co-monomer in SBR, incorporated at 23% to 25% by weight to improve stiffness, processability, and abrasion resistance. Acrylonitrile (C₃H₃N) : A co-monomer in NBR at 18% to 50% by weight, where higher content directly increases oil and fuel resistance. Chloroprene (C₄H₅Cl) : The monomer for neoprene rubber, where the chlorine atom imparts flame resistance and weather resistance to the polymer chain. Sulfur (Vulcanizing Agent) : Crosslinks polymer chains during vulcanization at 140°C to 200°C, converting uncured rubber into a thermoset elastomer. Carbon Black : A reinforcing filler added at 20% to 50% by weight that increases tensile strength and abrasion resistance by up to 10 times compared to unfilled rubber. Processing Oils : Paraffinic, naphthenic, or aromatic oils added at 5% to 30% by weight to reduce compound viscosity and modify cured rubber flexibility. Is Oil a Key Raw Material in Synthetic Rubber? Oil is a key raw material in synthetic rubber. Petroleum oil serves two distinct roles: as the primary feedstock for monomer generation through crude oil refining and steam cracking, and as a processing oil additive incorporated directly into rubber compounds during compounding. Crude oil naphtha is cracked at 750°C to 900°C to yield butadiene, ethylene, and propylene, as well as aromatics used to synthesize styrene, which forms the polymer backbone of synthetic rubber as a feedstock. Petroleum-derived processing oils are blended into the rubber matrix at 5% to 30% by weight to improve uncured compound flow and control stiffness of the cured product as a compound additive. Aromatic oils are preferred in SBR tire compounds, though concerns over polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) content have driven a shift to treated distillate aromatic extract (TDAE) oils compliant with EU Directive 2005/69/EC. How Is Synthetic Rubber Produced? Synthetic rubber is produced through a four-stage industrial process: monomer production, polymerization, compounding, and vulcanization. Each stage transforms raw petrochemical feedstocks into a finished elastomeric material with defined mechanical and chemical properties. Monomer production begins with steam cracking naphtha or ethane at 750°C to 900°C, yielding reactive monomers purified to 99%+ purity before polymerization. Polymerization converts monomers into long-chain polymers in stirred-tank or tubular reactors at 5°C to 80°C and 1 to 10 bar pressure. The resulting polymer is isolated, dried, and baled into crumb or slab form. At the compounding stage, the base polymer is blended with carbon black, process oils, sulfur, and accelerators in internal mixers to produce a homogeneous compound. Vulcanization cures the compound in heated molds at 140°C to 200°C under 1 to 15 MPa pressure, permanently crosslinking the polymer chains into the finished elastomer. What Is the Basic Process Used in Synthetic Rubber Manufacturing? The basic process in synthetic rubber manufacturing follows a sequential chemical and mechanical workflow from monomer synthesis to vulcanized rubber fabrication. Follow the five steps. First, petroleum feedstocks undergo steam cracking at 750°C to 900°C to produce reactive monomers. Second, the purified monomers enter polymerization reactors where free-radical, anionic, or coordination catalysts initiate chain-growth reactions at 5°C to 80°C. Third, the polymerization reaction is terminated with a shortstop chemical (hydroxylamine or sodium dimethyldithiocarbamate) once the target conversion rate of 60% to 72% is reached in emulsion systems. Fourth, the latex is coagulated using salt-acid mixtures, and the crumb rubber is washed, dried at 100°C to 130°C, and baled at 25 to 35 kilograms per bale. Fifth, the dried rubber is delivered to compounders who blend it with functional additives on internal mixers at 60°C to 160°C, producing the final compound ready for molding, extrusion, or calendering. Is Polymerization the Main Chemical Process Used? Polymerization is the main chemical process used in synthetic rubber production. The process chemically links individual monomer molecules into long polymer chains with molecular weights from 100,000 to over 1,000,000 g/mol, creating the macromolecular structure responsible for rubber's elastic behavior. Three distinct methods apply across synthetic rubber manufacturing: emulsion polymerization (used for SBR and NBR), solution polymerization (used for polybutadiene and solution-SBR), and coordination polymerization (used for EPDM and cis-polyisoprene). Emulsion polymerization accounts for approximately 60% to 65% of global synthetic rubber polymerization capacity, conducted in water-based systems at 5°C (cold emulsion) to 50°C (hot emulsion). Solution polymerization uses hydrocarbon solvents and anionic catalysts to produce rubbers with more controlled microstructure and narrower molecular weight distribution, delivering superior performance in high-specification tire and industrial rubber applications. What Are the Different Types of Synthetic Rubber? The different types of synthetic rubber are listed below. Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : A copolymer of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene, used primarily in tire treads. Global production exceeds 5 million metric tons per year. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) : A copolymer of acrylonitrile and butadiene with acrylonitrile content from 18% to 50%, delivering outstanding oil and fuel resistance for automotive seals and O-rings. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : A chloroprene-based rubber with balanced oil, ozone, heat, and flame resistance across an operating temperature range of -40°C to 120°C. EPDM Rubber : A terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and diene monomer, providing outstanding weather, ozone, and UV resistance for roofing membranes and automotive seals. Butyl Rubber (IIR) : A copolymer of isobutylene and isoprene with the lowest gas permeability among commercial rubbers, used in tire inner tubes and pharmaceutical closures. Silicone Rubber : A polysiloxane elastomer operating from -60°C to 230°C for medical devices, food-grade seals, and high-temperature industrial applications. The broad category of types of synthetic rubber encompasses additional specialty elastomers engineered for extreme chemical, thermal, and mechanical environments. What Are the Main Types of Synthetic Rubber Used Today? The main types of synthetic rubber used today are listed below. Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : Accounts for approximately 30% of total global synthetic rubber production, dominating passenger car and light truck tire manufacturing for its abrasion resistance and processing versatility. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) : A homopolymer of butadiene blended with SBR in tire compounds at 20% to 40% BR ratios to improve rolling resistance and cold-temperature flexibility. EPDM Rubber : The primary synthetic rubber for automotive weather seals, window profiles, and roofing membranes, with global production exceeding 1.5 million metric tons annually. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) : The standard elastomer for oil-resistant seals, gaskets, and hoses in automotive, oil and gas, and industrial machinery applications. Silicone Rubber : Serves medical implants, food processing equipment, and high-temperature electrical insulation across healthcare, food safety, and electronics industries. Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE/TPR) : Processed as thermoplastics and performing as rubbers, used in overmolding, flexible components, and medical tubing at volumes exceeding 3 million metric tons per year globally. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : The preferred rubber for wetsuits, industrial hoses, and cable jacketing where balanced oil and weather resistance is required. Are Types of Synthetic Rubber Connected to Types of Synthetic Polymers? Types of synthetic rubber are connected to types of synthetic polymers. Every synthetic rubber is a synthetic polymer by definition, produced through the chemical polymerization of monomer molecules into long-chain macromolecular structures using industrial processes. The distinction lies in the elastic mechanical behavior of rubber-type polymers, which exhibit high elongation at break (100% to 800%) and glass transition temperatures (Tg) below room temperature, allowing flexibility at ambient conditions. Synthetic rubbers are classified within the broader polymer family as elastomers, a subcategory capable of large, reversible deformation through crosslinked three-dimensional networks. Non-elastomeric synthetic polymers like polystyrene lack a low Tg, while others like polyethylene and polypropylene possess a low Tg but exhibit semi-crystalline thermoplastic behavior rather than the amorphous, crosslinked network that defines rubber behavior. Advances in synthetic polymer chemistry, including metallocene catalysis and living polymerization, directly influence the development of new synthetic rubber grades. How Does Synthetic Rubber Compare With Natural Rubber? Synthetic rubber and natural rubber are elastomeric materials capable of large elastic deformation, but differ substantially in origin, consistency, chemical resistance, and performance under extreme conditions. Natural rubber, derived from the latex of Hevea brasiliensis, consists primarily of cis-1,4-polyisoprene and offers exceptional tensile strength up to 30 MPa unfilled, superior to most synthetic rubber grades. Synthetic rubber is produced under controlled industrial conditions, delivering greater batch-to-batch consistency and engineered properties (oil resistance, heat resistance, flame retardancy) that natural rubber cannot achieve through its fixed polymer structure. Natural rubber degrades under ozone, UV, oils, and temperatures above 80°C without modification, whereas EPDM, NBR, and silicone are specifically formulated for resistance to the same conditions. Natural rubber is preferred in aircraft tires and high-performance engineering applications, while synthetic rubber dominates automotive fuel systems, roofing membranes, and medical devices. Detailed property data is available for natural rubber. What Are the Key Differences Between Synthetic Rubber and Natural Rubber? The key differences between synthetic rubber and natural rubber are listed below. Origin : Natural rubber is harvested from Hevea brasiliensis trees in Southeast Asia, while synthetic rubber is manufactured from petroleum-derived monomers in industrial chemical plants, reducing geographic supply concentration risk. Tensile Strength : Natural rubber achieves unfilled tensile strength up to 30 MPa through strain-induced crystallization. Carbon-black-reinforced SBR reaches 20 to 25 MPa, and NBR reaches 15 to 25 MPa under optimized compounding. Oil Resistance : NBR with 28% to 45% acrylonitrile content limits volume swell to below 10% after 72-hour immersion in ASTM Reference Oil No. 3. Natural rubber swells excessively in oil contact, making it unsuitable for fuel system applications. Temperature Range : Silicone rubber operates from -60°C to 230°C, and EPDM from -50°C to 150°C, far exceeding natural rubber's practical upper service limit of approximately 80°C. Weather Resistance : EPDM and neoprene resist ozone concentrations of 100 pphm without cracking over 72-hour exposure at 40°C. Natural rubber cracks within hours under equivalent ozone conditions without protective compounding. Consistency: Synthetic rubber delivers batch-to-batch molecular weight variation below 5%, while natural rubber varies significantly depending on the wintering period (February to May) and geographic origin. Is Natural Rubber More Elastic Than Synthetic Rubber? Natural rubber is more elastic than most synthetic rubber grades. The high-cis microstructure of natural rubber polyisoprene (99.9% cis-1,4 content) produces strain-induced crystallization (SIC) under load, generating tensile strength values up to 30 MPa in unfilled compounds. No standard synthetic rubber achieves equivalent unfilled tensile strength through the same mechanism. Elongation at break of natural rubber reaches 700% to 800%, compared to SBR at 400% to 600%, NBR at 300% to 500%, and EPDM at 150% to 400%, depending on formulation. Resilience (rebound elasticity) of natural rubber reaches 70% to 80% at room temperature, outperforming SBR at 55% to 65% and NBR at 40% to 55%. For aircraft tires, bridge bearings, and seismic isolation pads where maximum elasticity and dynamic fatigue resistance are required, natural rubber remains the preferred elastomeric material. What Is Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) in Synthetic Rubber Materials? Thermoplastic rubber (TPR) is a class of synthetic rubber that combines the elastic performance of conventional vulcanized rubber with the melt-processability of thermoplastics, allowing processing on standard injection molding and extrusion equipment without chemical vulcanization. TPR achieves rubber-like behavior through physical crosslinks formed by hard polymer domains dispersed within a soft elastomeric matrix, rather than covalent sulfur crosslinks. The hard domains (polystyrene, polypropylene, or polyurethane) soften or melt at 150°C to 220°C, enabling reprocessing, while the soft elastomeric segments (polybutadiene, polyisoprene, or polyolefin) provide flexibility and elastic recovery at service temperatures. TPR operates across approximately -50°C to 120°C, depending on grade, with hardness ranging from 20 Shore A to 50 Shore D. Detailed material data for thermoplastic rubber (TPR) . What Is Silicone in Synthetic Rubber Materials Silicone rubber is a synthetic elastomer based on a polysiloxane polymer backbone, where alternating silicon and oxygen atoms (Si-O-Si) form the main chain with organic groups (methyl, vinyl, or phenyl) attached to the silicon atoms. The inorganic Si-O backbone distinguishes silicone from all carbon-backbone synthetic rubbers, conferring exceptional thermal stability, electrical insulating properties, and biocompatibility. Silicone rubber maintains mechanical properties across -60°C to 230°C for standard grades, and up to 300°C for specialty formulations. Tensile strength ranges from 4 to 12 MPa, with elongation at break of 100% to 700% and dielectric strength of 15 to 25 kV/mm for high-voltage electrical insulation applications. In medical applications, platinum-cured silicone meets USP Class VI and ISO 10993 biocompatibility standards for implantable devices, surgical tubing, and drug delivery components. What Is Neoprene in Synthetic Rubber Materials? Neoprene (polychloroprene) is a synthetic rubber produced by the free-radical polymerization of chloroprene monomer (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene, C₄H₅Cl), where the chlorine atom in the polymer chain provides resistance to oils, flames, ozone, and weathering. Neoprene was the first commercially successful synthetic rubber, developed by DuPont in 1931. Neoprene operates across -40°C to 120°C, delivering tensile strength of 10 to 25 MPa and elongation at break of 200% to 600% depending on formulation. The material achieves a limiting oxygen index (LOI) of approximately 26% to 28%, classifying it as a self-extinguishing rubber for flame-resistance applications. Primary applications include wetsuits, industrial hose liners, cable jacketing, automotive belts, and construction gaskets. The performance distinctions from silicone across sealing, thermal, and chemical resistance requirements are covered in detail in silicone vs. neoprene . Is Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR) Considered a Form of Synthetic Rubber? Thermoplastic rubber (TPR) is considered a form of synthetic rubber. TPR exhibits the elastic deformation and recovery characteristics that define rubber behavior, including elongation at break values of 300% to 700% and hardness ranging from 20 Shore A to 50 Shore D.. The material is manufactured entirely from synthetic petrochemical polymers through industrial polymerization processes. The primary distinction of TPR within the synthetic rubber category is its thermoplastic processing behavior: TPR softens and flows above 150°C to 220°C and recovers its elastomeric properties upon cooling, without requiring chemical vulcanization. Conventional synthetic rubbers (SBR, NBR, EPDM) require irreversible sulfur crosslinking during vulcanization, making them thermoset materials that cannot be remelted. TPR's reprocessability allows scrap material to be reground and reused, reducing manufacturing waste. Thermoplastic rubber (TPR) serves across footwear, medical device, automotive, and consumer product applications. What Are the Examples of Synthetic Rubber Materials? The examples of synthetic rubber materials are listed below. Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) : A copolymer of styrene and butadiene representing the highest-volume synthetic rubber globally, with production exceeding 5 million metric tons annually Neoprene (Polychloroprene) : A chloroprene-based rubber offering balanced oil, flame, and weather resistance Nitrile Rubber (NBR) : An acrylonitrile-butadiene copolymer with outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and fuels Butyl Rubber (IIR) : An isobutylene-isoprene copolymer with the lowest gas permeability among commercial rubbers EPDM Rubber : A terpolymer providing superior weather, ozone, and UV resistance Silicone Rubber: A polysiloxane elastomer with a service temperature range of -60°C to 230°C Polyurethane Rubber (PU Rubber) : A segmented polyurethane elastomer with the highest abrasion resistance among commercial rubbers Acrylonitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR Variant) : A high-ACN specialty grade formulated for extreme oil resistance above 36% acrylonitrile content Chloroprene Rubber : The polymer class forming the chemical basis of all neoprene products Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR/TPE) : A reprocessable elastomeric material combining rubber performance with thermoplastic processability 1. Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) Styrene-Butadiene Rubber (SBR) is the world's most widely produced synthetic rubber, a random copolymer of approximately 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene by weight, manufactured through emulsion or solution polymerization. SBR was developed as a replacement for natural rubber during World War II under the U.S. government's GR-S program and has dominated the global rubber market since the 1950s. SBR delivers tensile strength of 15 to 25 MPa in carbon-black-reinforced compounds, abrasion resistance 25% to 40% superior to natural rubber in tire tread applications, and an operating temperature range of -50°C to 100°C. Tire tread production accounts for approximately 65% to 70% of total SBR consumption globally. SBR is priced at approximately [$1.20 to $1.80] per kilogram for standard emulsion grades, offering cost-competitive performance with greater processing consistency than natural rubber across high-volume manufacturing operations. 2. Neoprene (Polychloroprene) Neoprene (polychloroprene) is a synthetic rubber produced from the polymerization of chloroprene monomer, first commercialized by DuPont in 1931 as the first practical synthetic rubber alternative to natural rubber. The chlorine content of polychloroprene (approximately 40% by weight) imparts flame resistance, oil resistance, and ozone resistance that distinguish neoprene from hydrocarbon-backbone rubbers. Neoprene operates across -40°C to 120°C, with tensile strength of 10 to 25 MPa and elongation at break of 200% to 600% depending on compound formulation. The limiting oxygen index (LOI) of 26% to 28% classifies it as a self-extinguishing rubber for flame-resistance applications. Primary uses include wetsuits (2 mm to 7 mm panels), industrial hose liners, cable jacketing, automotive belts, and construction gaskets. Neoprene rubber sheet is priced at [$3 to $12] per kilogram depending on grade and order volume. 3. Nitrile Rubber (NBR) Nitrile Rubber (NBR) is a synthetic copolymer of acrylonitrile and butadiene, produced through emulsion polymerization at acrylonitrile contents ranging from 18% to 50% by weight. The acrylonitrile level directly determines oil resistance and low-temperature flexibility, requiring the compounder to balance the two properties for each application. NBR with 28% to 33% acrylonitrile content delivers a practical balance of oil resistance and cold-temperature flexibility (glass transition temperature of approximately -35°C to -25°C) for automotive fuel system seals and O-rings. Tensile strength ranges from 15 to 25 MPa, with elongation at break of 300% to 500%. NBR resists petroleum oils with volume swell below 15% after 70-hour immersion at 100°C in ASTM Reference Oil No. 3. NBR compound is priced at [$2.00 to $4.50] per kilogram depending on acrylonitrile content and formulation. Butyl Rubber (IIR) Butyl Rubber (IIR) is a synthetic rubber produced through cationic polymerization of isobutylene (95% to 99%) and isoprene (1% to 5%) at -90°C to -100°C using aluminum chloride catalyst. The near-complete absence of unsaturation in the polymer backbone gives butyl rubber its defining characteristic: the lowest gas permeability of any commercially produced rubber. Butyl rubber's oxygen permeability is approximately 15 times lower than natural rubber and over 100 times lower than SBR at room temperature, making it standard for tire inner tubes, tubeless tire inner liners, and pharmaceutical vial stoppers. The operating temperature range spans -40°C to 120°C, with tensile strength of 10 to 20 MPa and elongation at break of 400% to 700%. Standard butyl rubber is priced at [$2.50 to $5.00] per kilogram, with halogenated variants (chlorobutyl and bromobutyl) at [$3.50 to $7.00] per kilogram. 5. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) Rubber EPDM rubber is a terpolymer elastomer produced from ethylene (45% to 75%), propylene (25% to 50%), and a diene monomer (ethylidene norbornene, dicyclopentadiene, or 1,4-hexadiene at 1% to 12%) through coordination polymerization using Ziegler-Natta or metallocene catalysts. The saturated backbone, with unsaturation confined to pendant diene side chains, provides outstanding resistance to ozone, weathering, UV radiation, and oxidative aging. EPDM operates across -50°C to 150°C in standard grades, and up to 175°C in heat-stabilized formulations. Tensile strength ranges from 7 to 20 MPa, and elongation at break spans 150% to 600%. EPDM dominates automotive door and window seals, roofing membranes (covering approximately 20% of U.S. flat roofing area), and electrical wire insulation. EPDM compound is priced at [$1.80 to $3.50] per kilogram for standard grades. 6. Silicone Rubber Silicone rubber is a synthetic elastomer based on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer, where the alternating silicon-oxygen (Si-O) backbone with methyl, vinyl, or phenyl substituents provides thermal stability, electrical insulation, and biocompatibility unmatched by carbon-backbone rubbers. The polymer is compounded with pyrogenic silica at 7% to 50% by weight as a reinforcing filler and cured through peroxide or platinum-catalyzed addition cure systems. Silicone rubber maintains elastomeric properties across -60°C to 230°C for general grades, and -100°C to 300°C for specialty phenyl and heat-stabilized methyl-vinyl grades. Tensile strength ranges from 4 to 12 MPa, with dielectric strength of 15 to 25 kV/mm for electrical insulation applications. Biocompatibility under USP Class VI and ISO 10993 standards qualifies silicone for implantable devices and food-contact applications. Silicone rubber compound is priced at [$8 to $35] per kilogram, depending on grade and purity level. 7. Polyurethane Rubber (PU Rubber) Polyurethane rubber (PU rubber) is a synthetic elastomer produced by the reaction of polyol and diisocyanate components, forming a segmented block copolymer with alternating hard (urethane) and soft (polyol) segments that delivers the highest abrasion resistance among commercially produced rubbers. The abrasion resistance, measured by the DIN 53516 test, reaches 20 to 80 mm³ volume loss, significantly superior to natural rubber (100 to 150 mm³) and SBR (100 to 180 mm³). PU rubber operates across -40°C to 90°C, with tensile strength of 20 to 55 MPa and elongation at break of 300% to 700%, delivering the best unfilled tensile performance among synthetic rubber types. Shore hardness ranges from 30 Shore A to 70 Shore D. Primary applications include industrial rollers, scraper blades, mining screens, skateboard wheels, and hydraulic seals. Raw PU rubber compound is priced at [$4 to $15] per kilogram. 8. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR Variant) Acrylonitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) in its high-ACN specialty variant is formulated with acrylonitrile content exceeding 36% by weight, producing an elastomer with extreme resistance to petroleum oils, aromatic fuels, and hydrocarbon solvents beyond standard NBR grades. At 36% to 50% acrylonitrile content, volume swell after 70-hour immersion in ASTM Reference Oil No. 3 at 100°C drops below 10%, compared to 20% to 30% for standard 28% ACN-grade NBR. High-ACN NBR variants are used in fuel injection system components, oil well equipment seals, and chemical-resistant gloves where standard NBR cannot meet aggressive fluid resistance requirements. The trade-off is reduced low-temperature flexibility, with glass transition temperature rising to -15°C to -5°C at high ACN content compared to -35°C for standard grades. High-ACN NBR is priced at [$3.50 to $6.00] per kilogram. Chloroprene Rubber Chloroprene rubber is the polymer class produced through free-radical emulsion polymerization of 2-chloro-1,3-butadiene (chloroprene) monomer, forming the chemical basis from which all neoprene products are derived. The chlorine substituent accounts for approximately 40% of the molecular weight per repeat unit, imparting polar character that resists non-polar hydrocarbon fluids and aliphatic oils. Chloroprene rubber is produced in grades differentiated by molecular weight distribution, crystallization rate, and Mooney viscosity (ML(1+4) at 100°C from 30 to 120 MU) for extrusion, calendering, compression molding, and injection molding applications. Tensile strength of compounded chloroprene rubber reaches 10 to 25 MPa, with an operating temperature range of -40°C to 120°C. Applications include automotive drive belts, industrial hoses, bridge bearing pads, cable jacketing, and adhesive formulations. Raw chloroprene rubber is priced at [$3.00 to $6.50] per kilogram. "When integrating an elastomeric component into a larger mechanical assembly, engineers must design for the material's unyielding volumetric behavior under compression rather than treating it like a highly forgiving plastic. Successful assembly optimization relies on providing adequate void space for gland fill and accounting for the broader tolerances characteristic of flexible materials (using targeted GD&T strategy). Failing to respect these physical boundaries invariably leads to warped mating hardware, joint gaps, or premature seal failure." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering 10. Thermoplastic Rubber (TPR / TPE) Thermoplastic rubber (TPR), synonymously referred to as thermoplastic elastomer (TPE), achieves rubber-like elasticity through physical rather than chemical crosslinking, allowing processing on conventional injection molding equipment at 180°C to 220°C and reprocessing from scrap without property degradation. TPR encompasses several polymer families: styrenic block copolymers (SBS, SEBS), thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers (TPO), thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), thermoplastic vulcanizates (TPV), and thermoplastic polyester elastomers (TPEE). Hardness ranges from 20 Shore A to 50 Shore D across the TPR/TPE family, with tensile strength of 5 to 40 MPa depending on the polymer system. Applications include overmolded grips, medical tubing, footwear soles, automotive interior trim, and flexible consumer product components. TPR material is commercially priced at [$2.50 to $10.00] per kilogram, depending on polymer family and hardness grade. What Are the Advantages of Using Synthetic Rubber? The advantages of using synthetic rubber are listed below. Engineered Chemical Resistance : NBR with 36% acrylonitrile content limits volume swell to below 10% in ASTM Reference Oil No. 3 at 100°C, qualifying it for direct fuel system contact where natural rubber is unsuitable. Extended Temperature Range : Silicone rubber operates from -60°C to 230°C and EPDM from -50°C to 150°C, far exceeding natural rubber's practical service limit of approximately 80°C. Consistent Supply : Synthetic rubber production is distributed across petrochemical facilities in North America, Europe, and Asia, reducing the geographic supply concentration risk associated with natural rubber sourced primarily from Southeast Asia. Batch-to-Batch Consistency: Synthetic rubber polymerization delivers molecular weight variation below 5% from batch to batch, compared to natural rubber, where molecular weight varies significantly by the wintering period (February to May) and geographic origin. Flame and Ozone Resistance : Neoprene achieves a limiting oxygen index of 26% to 28%, and EPDM resists ozone concentrations of 100 pphm without cracking over 72-hour exposure at 40°C. Reprocessability (TPR/TPE) : Thermoplastic rubber grades are remelted from production scrap, reducing material waste by 15% to 30% in injection molding operations compared to thermoset rubber compounds.
