Hydraulic Press Systems: Provide the clamping force that holds the die halves together during pressurization, preventing die separation under internal fluid pressure loads. High-Pressure Pumps: Generate and deliver hydraulic fluid at the pressures required for metal forming, ranging from 50 MPa to over 400 MPa, depending on the application. Pressure Intensifiers: Amplify hydraulic system pressure to levels beyond standard pump output, enabling high-pressure hydroforming of strong or thick materials. Sealed Die Systems: Enclose the workpiece and contain the hydraulic fluid during forming, defining the final part geometry through precision-machined cavity surfaces. Bladder or Diaphragm Systems: Flexible membranes that contain and transmit fluid pressure uniformly against sheet metal workpieces in sheet hydroforming setups. Tube Sealing Rams: Hydraulic cylinders that seal the open ends of tubes and apply axial feed force during internal pressurization in tube hydroforming operations. How Do Hydroforming Dies Shape the Metal? Hydroforming dies shape the metal by defining the precise external geometry that the pressurized workpiece must conform to during forming. The die cavity surfaces act as a rigid boundary against which the expanding metal presses under hydraulic force. As internal pressure rises, the metal flows outward until full contact with every contour of the die cavity is achieved. Die geometry determines the final dimensions, cross-sectional profile, and surface detail of the formed part. The materials are tool steel or hardened alloy steel to withstand repeated high-pressure forming cycles without dimensional wear. Precision machining of die cavity surfaces ensures tight tolerances in the finished part. Lubricant applied to the workpiece reduces friction between the metal and die walls, improving material flow and surface finish during forming. Proper die alignment prevents uneven pressure loading and reduces defects such as wrinkles, thinning, or incomplete forming. Venting features help trapped air escape from the cavity, allowing the metal to contact the die surfaces fully. Regular die inspection detects wear, surface damage, or dimensional changes that affect part accuracy during repeated production cycles. Does Hydraulic Fluid Act as a Forming Tool? Yes, hydraulic fluid acts as a uniform pressure medium that replaces rigid mechanical punch contact in hydroforming. The fluid transmits forming force evenly across every point of the workpiece surface simultaneously. Uniform pressure distribution enables smoother stress distribution compared to localized punch contact in conventional stamping. Material flows more evenly under fluid pressure because no single contact point concentrates force on the workpiece. The fluid conforms to the shape of the workpiece surface without introducing localized friction or stress concentration. Improved material flow results in better dimensional accuracy, smoother surface finish, and reduced risk of tearing in formed parts. Controlled fluid pressure supports gradual deformation, which helps maintain wall thickness more consistently across complex shapes. Hydraulic fluid, therefore, plays a direct role in forming precision, defect reduction, and overall process stability. What Are the Advantages of Hydroforming? The advantages of hydroforming are listed below. Improved Strain Distribution: Uniform fluid pressure spreads, forming strain evenly across the workpiece, reducing localized thinning and improving part consistency. Complex Geometry Capability: Hydroforming produces smooth curves, variable cross-sections, and intricate profiles in a single forming cycle without multiple tooling stages. Reduced Weld Joints: Single-piece hydroformed structures replace multi-part welded assemblies, reducing assembly time and improving structural integrity. Lightweight Structural Optimization: Thinner walls and optimized cross-sections are achievable without sacrificing strength, supporting weight reduction goals in automotive and aerospace design. High Dimensional Accuracy: Controlled pressure cycles and precision die surfaces produce parts with tight tolerances and repeatable geometry across production runs. Lower Tooling Contact Stress: Fluid pressure replaces direct punch contact, reducing die wear and surface marking compared to conventional stamping operations. How Does Hydroforming Improve Structural Strength? Hydroforming improves structural strength by producing parts with uniform wall thickness, reduced stress concentrations, and strain-hardened material properties resulting from controlled plastic deformation. The forming process work hardens the metal as it deforms, increasing yield strength in the finished part compared to the raw material. Eliminating weld joints removes the weakest points in welded assemblies, improving fatigue resistance and load-bearing capacity. Complex closed cross sections formed in a single hydroforming cycle provide greater torsional stiffness than open or multi-part welded sections. Automotive frame rails and structural tubes benefit from the combination of optimized geometry and work-hardened material. Consistent wall thickness distribution across the part ensures that no single region becomes a failure point under operational loading. Smooth material flow improves impact performance because stress spreads across the formed structure more evenly. Reduced part count creates stronger assemblies by limiting seams, joints, and connection points that weaken under repeated loads. Does Hydroforming Reduce Welding Requirements? Yes, hydroforming enables single-piece structures that replace multiple welded components in assemblies. The process forms complex geometries from one continuous piece of metal, eliminating the need for joining separate stamped sections. Fewer weld joints improve fatigue resistance because welds introduce residual stresses and heat-affected zones that reduce material strength. Assembly complexity decreases when fewer individual parts require joining, lowering labor time and the risk of misalignment. Structural integrity improves in components subjected to cyclic loading, as the absence of welds removes potential crack initiation sites. Automotive chassis and exhaust system manufacturers apply hydroforming specifically to reduce weld count in safety-critical structural assemblies. Single-piece hydroformed parts improve dimensional consistency because fewer joined sections shift during assembly. Reduced joining requirements support cleaner load paths across the finished component, improving strength under bending, torsion, and vibration. What Are the Applications of Hydroforming? The applications of hydroforming are listed below. Automotive Chassis Components: Frame rails, engine cradles, roof rails, and A-pillars are hydroformed to achieve high stiffness, reduced weight, and fewer weld joints in vehicle body structures. Aerospace Structural Tubing: Lightweight tubular frames, engine cowlings, aerospace ducting, and minor frame brackets use hydroformed titanium and aluminum alloys to meet strength-to-weight requirements in aircraft design. Bicycle Frames: Aluminum and steel bicycle frame tubes are hydroformed to produce complex tapered and multi-profile cross-sections that improve stiffness and aerodynamic performance. Exhaust Systems: Automotive exhaust pipes, manifolds, and catalytic converter housings use hydroformed stainless steel tubes to achieve smooth bends and accurate fitment. HVAC Tubing Systems: Heating and cooling ductwork uses hydroformed aluminum or steel tubing to produce complex routing paths with minimal joints and leak points. Industrial Fluid and Gas Piping: High-pressure piping systems for fluid and gas transport use hydroformed components to achieve consistent wall thickness and reliable sealing geometry. Why Is Hydroforming Important in Automotive Lightweight Design? Hydroforming is a key process in automotive lightweight design because it produces high-strength structural components with thinner walls and fewer joints than conventional welded assemblies. The process allows engineers to form closed tubular cross-sections with variable geometry along their length, optimizing material placement for load distribution. Weight reduction in body-in-white structures directly lowers vehicle mass, improving fuel consumption in combustion vehicles and extending operating range in electric vehicles. Hydroformed components replace multiple stamped and welded parts in frame structures, reducing part count and assembly complexity. Aluminum and high-strength steel hydroforming enable equivalent structural performance at lower mass than conventional mild steel stampings. The ability to form complex geometry in a single operation reduces tooling investment and manufacturing steps compared to multi-part welded designs. Are Hydroformed Parts Lighter Than Welded Assemblies? Yes, hydroformed parts are lighter than equivalent welded assemblies in most structural applications. Reduced weld joints and optimized material distribution lower the total mass of the finished structure. Single-piece hydroformed components eliminate the overlap and joint reinforcement material required in welded assemblies. Wall thickness optimization across the formed cross-section places material only where structural loads demand it, avoiding excess weight. Weight reduction improves fuel efficiency in combustion vehicles and extends range in electric vehicles. Aerospace and automotive manufacturers prioritize hydroforming specifically because the mass savings deliver measurable performance and efficiency benefits in transport applications. Lower part count reduces brackets, fasteners, and secondary reinforcements that add unnecessary mass. Hydroforming supports lightweight design without sacrificing stiffness because closed-section shapes distribute loads efficiently. How Does Hydroforming Compare to Deep Drawing Stamping? Hydroforming and deep draw stamping both form sheet metal into three-dimensional shapes, but the two processes differ fundamentally in how forming force is applied. Deep draw stamping uses a rigid mechanical punch that forces the blank into a die cavity through direct contact, concentrating stress at the punch-to-blank contact zone. Hydroforming replaces the rigid punch with hydraulic fluid pressure, distributing forming force uniformly across the entire blank surface. The uniform pressure in hydroforming reduces localized thinning and allows deeper draws without fracture compared to conventional stamping. Deep drawing stamping is more economical for high-volume production of simpler geometries because tooling costs are lower and cycle times are faster. Hydroforming achieves better surface finish, tighter tolerances, and greater geometric complexity in a single operation, but at higher equipment and tooling costs. Part depth, geometry complexity, and production volume determine which process offers better value for a specific application involving Deep Drawing Stamping . What Is the Difference Between Hydroforming and Mechanical Stamping? Hydroforming and mechanical stamping differ primarily in the forming mechanism, stress distribution, and geometric capability. Mechanical stamping applies force through rigid punch and die contact, concentrating stress at the tooling interface and limiting the complexity of formable shapes. Hydroforming uses hydraulic fluid pressure as the forming medium, distributing force uniformly across the workpiece without direct mechanical contact. Hydroforming achieves deeper draws, smoother surface finishes, and more complex cross-sections than mechanical stamping in a single forming stage. Mechanical stamping requires multiple progressive die stages to form complex parts that hydroforming produces in one cycle. Tooling costs for hydroforming are higher, but part consolidation reduces overall assembly costs. Mechanical stamping remains faster and more economical for simple, high-volume parts where geometric complexity is not a requirement. Is Hydroforming Better for Complex Geometries? Yes, hydroforming is better suited for complex and smooth geometries due to uniform fluid pressure distribution across the entire workpiece surface. Rigid tooling in mechanical stamping concentrates stress at punch contact zones, limiting the depth and complexity of formable shapes. Fluid pressure conforms to the workpiece geometry without introducing localized deformation failure at specific contact points. Complex cross sections, variable wall profiles, and smooth compound curves are achievable in a single hydroforming cycle. Reduced localized deformation failure means fewer rejected parts and lower scrap rates in complex geometry production. Industries requiring tight tolerances and multi-profile components consistently select hydroforming over rigid tooling processes for geometrically demanding applications. Smooth pressure application improves surface finish by reducing tool marks and abrupt strain transitions. Hydroforming supports cleaner part geometry because the metal follows the die contours with fewer wrinkles, seams, or sharp distortions. What Are the Limitations of Hydroforming? Hydroforming presents several limitations that restrict its application in certain manufacturing contexts. Equipment and tooling costs are significantly higher than conventional stamping, requiring substantial capital investment for hydraulic press systems, high-pressure pumps, and precision dies. Cycle times are longer than mechanical stamping because pressurization and pressure regulation add time to each forming operation, reducing throughput in high-volume production. Material selection is constrained by ductility requirements, excluding brittle or low-elongation materials that fracture under hydraulic pressure. Geometry is limited to shapes achievable within a sealed die cavity, making certain open or reentrant profiles impossible to form. Process control demands are high, as precise pressure regulation and sealing integrity are critical to avoiding burst failure and dimensional inaccuracy. Hydroforming is cost-effective for medium-volume, geometrically complex parts where part consolidation offsets the higher per-cycle cost. Maintenance requirements are higher because seals, pumps, dies, and pressure control systems operate under demanding loads. Prototype development requires detailed forming simulations and trial runs to identify thinning, wrinkling, or bursting risks before production. Skilled operators and engineers remain necessary because pressure timing, lubrication, material feed, and die alignment directly affect part quality. Why Is Hydroforming Limited to Certain Materials and Thicknesses? Hydroforming is limited to certain materials and thicknesses because the process relies on plastic deformation under fluid pressure, which requires adequate ductility and elongation in the workpiece material. Brittle materials fracture before reaching the plastic deformation range needed to conform to die geometry. Very thick sections require extremely high pressure to achieve sufficient forming force, exceeding the practical limits of most hydraulic press systems. Thin-walled materials risk buckling or wrinkling under axial feed forces in tube hydroforming if the wall thickness falls below the minimum required for the tube diameter. Material thickness uniformity affects pressure distribution and forming consistency, making materials with significant thickness variation unsuitable for tight-tolerance applications. High-strength materials with limited elongation, such as hardened tool steels, resist plastic deformation at achievable pressure levels and are excluded from standard hydroforming operations. Can Hydroforming Replace All Sheet Metal Forming Processes? No, hydroforming is not suitable for all geometries or cost-sensitive high-volume production environments. Conventional stamping remains more economical for simpler parts at scale because tooling costs are lower and cycle times are faster. Hydroforming requires sealed die systems, high-pressure fluid management, and longer cycle times that increase per-part cost relative to stamping in large production runs. Simple flat or single-curvature parts offer no geometric advantage from hydroforming and are produced more efficiently through conventional sheet metal processes. Re-entrant geometries and open-profile shapes that cannot be enclosed in a die cavity are outside the scope of hydroforming entirely. The process complements rather than replaces conventional forming methods, addressing the specific subset of applications where geometric complexity and part consolidation justify the higher process cost for Sheet Metal . Final inspection checks the thickness distribution, surface quality, and dimensional accuracy before the formed panel moves to trimming or assembly. Is Tube Hydroforming Common in Automotive Manufacturing? Yes, tube hydroforming is widely used in automotive structural components (frame rails, engine cradles, A-pillars, and exhaust systems). The process reduces the number of weld joints required to assemble complex tubular structures. Fewer welds improve structural rigidity and fatigue resistance in load-bearing automotive components. Hydroformed frame rails achieve better torsional stiffness than welded assemblies of equivalent weight. The process enables weight reduction by forming complex cross-sections from a single tube rather than multiple stamped and welded parts. Automotive manufacturers apply tube hydroforming across passenger vehicle platforms and commercial vehicle chassis systems. Consistent wall thickness helps maintain crash performance in safety-critical structural areas. Complex tube shapes improve packaging space around engines, suspension parts, and exhaust routing. Reduced part count lowers assembly complexity and supports repeatable production quality. What Materials Are Used in Hydroforming? The materials that are used in hydroforming are listed below. Low-Carbon Steel: Offers high ductility and consistent formability, making it a standard material for automotive structural hydroforming applications. HSLA Steel: High-strength low-alloy steel provides greater strength-to-weight ratios than mild steel, supporting lightweight structural designs in automotive and industrial applications. Stainless Steel: Provides corrosion resistance alongside adequate ductility for exhaust systems, food processing equipment, and HVAC components. Aluminum Alloys: Lightweight and corrosion-resistant, aluminum alloys are common in automotive body panels and aerospace structural tubes where weight reduction is a priority. Copper Alloys: Applied in limited situations requiring electrical conductivity or corrosion resistance (plumbing fittings and heat exchanger tubing). Titanium Alloys: Used in aerospace-specific applications where high strength, low weight, and extreme temperature resistance are required, though higher cost limits broader use. For design engineers, optimizing the relationship between material elongation metrics, variable cross-sections, and dynamic internal pressure pathways is vital to avoiding localized thin-out or buckling failure modes. Ultimately, successful deployment comes down to understanding fluid mechanics as a predictable, highly repeatable forming tool." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering What Material Properties Are Required for Hydroforming? Hydroforming requires materials with high ductility, adequate tensile strength, and consistent elongation properties to undergo significant plastic deformation without premature failure. Elongation at fracture above 20% is generally preferred for sheet and tube hydroforming applications. Low yield to tensile strength ratios allow the material to deform plastically over a wide strain range before reaching failure limits. Work hardening behavior affects how the material responds to increasing strain during forming. Materials with gradual strain hardening distribute deformation more evenly, reducing the risk of localized thinning. Surface quality and thickness uniformity in the raw material directly influence dimensional accuracy in the finished hydroformed part. Consistent mechanical properties across the material batch are necessary to maintain repeatable forming results in production environments. Aluminum, stainless steel, low carbon steel, brass, and copper are common hydroforming materials because each metal offers useful ductility. Poor ductility increases tearing risk during expansion, especially in corners and high-strain areas. Proper material testing before production helps confirm formability, thickness behavior, and failure limits. Are Ductile Metals Better for Hydroforming? Yes, ductile metals are preferred for hydroforming because ductile metals undergo significant plastic deformation without cracking under applied fluid pressure. High elongation values allow the metal to stretch and conform to complex die geometries without fracturing. Formability, defined by a material’s ability to deform plastically without failure, is the primary selection criterion for hydroforming materials. Metals with low ductility fracture at lower strain levels, limiting the complexity of shapes achievable. The examples of ductile materials that perform well in hydroforming include low-carbon steel, aluminum alloys, and copper alloys, all of which offer the combination of elongation and formability that the process demands. Consistent grain structure improves forming stability by helping strain distribute evenly across the workpiece. Proper material testing confirms whether the selected metal meets pressure, elongation, and thickness requirements before production using Ductile Metals . What Equipment Is Used in Hydroforming? The equipment that is used in hydroforming is listed below. Hydraulic Press Systems: Provide the clamping force that holds the die halves together during pressurization, preventing die separation under internal fluid pressure loads. High-Pressure Pumps: Generate and deliver hydraulic fluid at the pressures required for metal forming, ranging from 50 MPa to over 400 MPa, depending on the application. Pressure Intensifiers: Amplify hydraulic system pressure to levels beyond standard pump output, enabling high-pressure hydroforming of strong or thick materials. Sealed Die Systems: Enclose the workpiece and contain the hydraulic fluid during forming, defining the final part geometry through precision-machined cavity surfaces. Bladder or Diaphragm Systems: Flexible membranes that contain and transmit fluid pressure uniformly against sheet metal workpieces in sheet hydroforming setups. Tube Sealing Rams: Hydraulic cylinders that seal the open ends of tubes and apply axial feed force during internal pressurization in tube hydroforming operations. How Do Hydroforming Dies Shape the Metal? Hydroforming dies shape the metal by defining the precise external geometry that the pressurized workpiece must conform to during forming. The die cavity surfaces act as a rigid boundary against which the expanding metal presses under hydraulic force. As internal pressure rises, the metal flows outward until full contact with every contour of the die cavity is achieved. Die geometry determines the final dimensions, cross-sectional profile, and surface detail of the formed part. The materials are tool steel or hardened alloy steel to withstand repeated high-pressure forming cycles without dimensional wear. Precision machining of die cavity surfaces ensures tight tolerances in the finished part. Lubricant applied to the workpiece reduces friction between the metal and die walls, improving material flow and surface finish during forming. Proper die alignment prevents uneven pressure loading and reduces defects such as wrinkles, thinning, or incomplete forming. Venting features help trapped air escape from the cavity, allowing the metal to contact the die surfaces fully. Regular die inspection detects wear, surface damage, or dimensional changes that affect part accuracy during repeated production cycles. Does Hydraulic Fluid Act as a Forming Tool? Yes, hydraulic fluid acts as a uniform pressure medium that replaces rigid mechanical punch contact in hydroforming. The fluid transmits forming force evenly across every point of the workpiece surface simultaneously. Uniform pressure distribution enables smoother stress distribution compared to localized punch contact in conventional stamping. Material flows more evenly under fluid pressure because no single contact point concentrates force on the workpiece. The fluid conforms to the shape of the workpiece surface without introducing localized friction or stress concentration. Improved material flow results in better dimensional accuracy, smoother surface finish, and reduced risk of tearing in formed parts. Controlled fluid pressure supports gradual deformation, which helps maintain wall thickness more consistently across complex shapes. Hydraulic fluid, therefore, plays a direct role in forming precision, defect reduction, and overall process stability. What Are the Advantages of Hydroforming? The advantages of hydroforming are listed below. Improved Strain Distribution: Uniform fluid pressure spreads, forming strain evenly across the workpiece, reducing localized thinning and improving part consistency. Complex Geometry Capability: Hydroforming produces smooth curves, variable cross-sections, and intricate profiles in a single forming cycle without multiple tooling stages. Reduced Weld Joints: Single-piece hydroformed structures replace multi-part welded assemblies, reducing assembly time and improving structural integrity. Lightweight Structural Optimization: Thinner walls and optimized cross-sections are achievable without sacrificing strength, supporting weight reduction goals in automotive and aerospace design. High Dimensional Accuracy: Controlled pressure cycles and precision die surfaces produce parts with tight tolerances and repeatable geometry across production runs. Lower Tooling Contact Stress: Fluid pressure replaces direct punch contact, reducing die wear and surface marking compared to conventional stamping operations. How Does Hydroforming Improve Structural Strength? Hydroforming improves structural strength by producing parts with uniform wall thickness, reduced stress concentrations, and strain-hardened material properties resulting from controlled plastic deformation. The forming process work hardens the metal as it deforms, increasing yield strength in the finished part compared to the raw material. Eliminating weld joints removes the weakest points in welded assemblies, improving fatigue resistance and load-bearing capacity. Complex closed cross sections formed in a single hydroforming cycle provide greater torsional stiffness than open or multi-part welded sections. Automotive frame rails and structural tubes benefit from the combination of optimized geometry and work-hardened material. Consistent wall thickness distribution across the part ensures that no single region becomes a failure point under operational loading. Smooth material flow improves impact performance because stress spreads across the formed structure more evenly. Reduced part count creates stronger assemblies by limiting seams, joints, and connection points that weaken under repeated loads. Does Hydroforming Reduce Welding Requirements? Yes, hydroforming enables single-piece structures that replace multiple welded components in assemblies. The process forms complex geometries from one continuous piece of metal, eliminating the need for joining separate stamped sections. Fewer weld joints improve fatigue resistance because welds introduce residual stresses and heat-affected zones that reduce material strength. Assembly complexity decreases when fewer individual parts require joining, lowering labor time and the risk of misalignment. Structural integrity improves in components subjected to cyclic loading, as the absence of welds removes potential crack initiation sites. Automotive chassis and exhaust system manufacturers apply hydroforming specifically to reduce weld count in safety-critical structural assemblies. Single-piece hydroformed parts improve dimensional consistency because fewer joined sections shift during assembly. Reduced joining requirements support cleaner load paths across the finished component, improving strength under bending, torsion, and vibration. What Are the Applications of Hydroforming? The applications of hydroforming are listed below. Automotive Chassis Components: Frame rails, engine cradles, roof rails, and A-pillars are hydroformed to achieve high stiffness, reduced weight, and fewer weld joints in vehicle body structures. Aerospace Structural Tubing: Lightweight tubular frames, engine cowlings, aerospace ducting, and minor frame brackets use hydroformed titanium and aluminum alloys to meet strength-to-weight requirements in aircraft design. Bicycle Frames: Aluminum and steel bicycle frame tubes are hydroformed to produce complex tapered and multi-profile cross-sections that improve stiffness and aerodynamic performance. Exhaust Systems: Automotive exhaust pipes, manifolds, and catalytic converter housings use hydroformed stainless steel tubes to achieve smooth bends and accurate fitment. HVAC Tubing Systems: Heating and cooling ductwork uses hydroformed aluminum or steel tubing to produce complex routing paths with minimal joints and leak points. Industrial Fluid and Gas Piping: High-pressure piping systems for fluid and gas transport use hydroformed components to achieve consistent wall thickness and reliable sealing geometry. Why Is Hydroforming Important in Automotive Lightweight Design? Hydroforming is a key process in automotive lightweight design because it produces high-strength structural components with thinner walls and fewer joints than conventional welded assemblies. The process allows engineers to form closed tubular cross-sections with variable geometry along their length, optimizing material placement for load distribution. Weight reduction in body-in-white structures directly lowers vehicle mass, improving fuel consumption in combustion vehicles and extending operating range in electric vehicles. Hydroformed components replace multiple stamped and welded parts in frame structures, reducing part count and assembly complexity. Aluminum and high-strength steel hydroforming enable equivalent structural performance at lower mass than conventional mild steel stampings. The ability to form complex geometry in a single operation reduces tooling investment and manufacturing steps compared to multi-part welded designs. Are Hydroformed Parts Lighter Than Welded Assemblies? Yes, hydroformed parts are lighter than equivalent welded assemblies in most structural applications. Reduced weld joints and optimized material distribution lower the total mass of the finished structure. Single-piece hydroformed components eliminate the overlap and joint reinforcement material required in welded assemblies. Wall thickness optimization across the formed cross-section places material only where structural loads demand it, avoiding excess weight. Weight reduction improves fuel efficiency in combustion vehicles and extends range in electric vehicles. Aerospace and automotive manufacturers prioritize hydroforming specifically because the mass savings deliver measurable performance and efficiency benefits in transport applications. Lower part count reduces brackets, fasteners, and secondary reinforcements that add unnecessary mass. Hydroforming supports lightweight design without sacrificing stiffness because closed-section shapes distribute loads efficiently. How Does Hydroforming Compare to Deep Drawing Stamping? Hydroforming and deep draw stamping both form sheet metal into three-dimensional shapes, but the two processes differ fundamentally in how forming force is applied. Deep draw stamping uses a rigid mechanical punch that forces the blank into a die cavity through direct contact, concentrating stress at the punch-to-blank contact zone. Hydroforming replaces the rigid punch with hydraulic fluid pressure, distributing forming force uniformly across the entire blank surface. The uniform pressure in hydroforming reduces localized thinning and allows deeper draws without fracture compared to conventional stamping. Deep drawing stamping is more economical for high-volume production of simpler geometries because tooling costs are lower and cycle times are faster. Hydroforming achieves better surface finish, tighter tolerances, and greater geometric complexity in a single operation, but at higher equipment and tooling costs. Part depth, geometry complexity, and production volume determine which process offers better value for a specific application involving Deep Drawing Stamping . What Is the Difference Between Hydroforming and Mechanical Stamping? Hydroforming and mechanical stamping differ primarily in the forming mechanism, stress distribution, and geometric capability. Mechanical stamping applies force through rigid punch and die contact, concentrating stress at the tooling interface and limiting the complexity of formable shapes. Hydroforming uses hydraulic fluid pressure as the forming medium, distributing force uniformly across the workpiece without direct mechanical contact. Hydroforming achieves deeper draws, smoother surface finishes, and more complex cross-sections than mechanical stamping in a single forming stage. Mechanical stamping requires multiple progressive die stages to form complex parts that hydroforming produces in one cycle. Tooling costs for hydroforming are higher, but part consolidation reduces overall assembly costs. Mechanical stamping remains faster and more economical for simple, high-volume parts where geometric complexity is not a requirement. Is Hydroforming Better for Complex Geometries? Yes, hydroforming is better suited for complex and smooth geometries due to uniform fluid pressure distribution across the entire workpiece surface. Rigid tooling in mechanical stamping concentrates stress at punch contact zones, limiting the depth and complexity of formable shapes. Fluid pressure conforms to the workpiece geometry without introducing localized deformation failure at specific contact points. Complex cross sections, variable wall profiles, and smooth compound curves are achievable in a single hydroforming cycle. Reduced localized deformation failure means fewer rejected parts and lower scrap rates in complex geometry production. Industries requiring tight tolerances and multi-profile components consistently select hydroforming over rigid tooling processes for geometrically demanding applications. Smooth pressure application improves surface finish by reducing tool marks and abrupt strain transitions. Hydroforming supports cleaner part geometry because the metal follows the die contours with fewer wrinkles, seams, or sharp distortions. What Are the Limitations of Hydroforming? Hydroforming presents several limitations that restrict its application in certain manufacturing contexts. Equipment and tooling costs are significantly higher than conventional stamping, requiring substantial capital investment for hydraulic press systems, high-pressure pumps, and precision dies. Cycle times are longer than mechanical stamping because pressurization and pressure regulation add time to each forming operation, reducing throughput in high-volume production. Material selection is constrained by ductility requirements, excluding brittle or low-elongation materials that fracture under hydraulic pressure. Geometry is limited to shapes achievable within a sealed die cavity, making certain open or reentrant profiles impossible to form. Process control demands are high, as precise pressure regulation and sealing integrity are critical to avoiding burst failure and dimensional inaccuracy. Hydroforming is cost-effective for medium-volume, geometrically complex parts where part consolidation offsets the higher per-cycle cost. Maintenance requirements are higher because seals, pumps, dies, and pressure control systems operate under demanding loads. Prototype development requires detailed forming simulations and trial runs to identify thinning, wrinkling, or bursting risks before production. Skilled operators and engineers remain necessary because pressure timing, lubrication, material feed, and die alignment directly affect part quality. Why Is Hydroforming Limited to Certain Materials and Thicknesses? Hydroforming is limited to certain materials and thicknesses because the process relies on plastic deformation under fluid pressure, which requires adequate ductility and elongation in the workpiece material. Brittle materials fracture before reaching the plastic deformation range needed to conform to die geometry. Very thick sections require extremely high pressure to achieve sufficient forming force, exceeding the practical limits of most hydraulic press systems. Thin-walled materials risk buckling or wrinkling under axial feed forces in tube hydroforming if the wall thickness falls below the minimum required for the tube diameter. Material thickness uniformity affects pressure distribution and forming consistency, making materials with significant thickness variation unsuitable for tight-tolerance applications. High-strength materials with limited elongation, such as hardened tool steels, resist plastic deformation at achievable pressure levels and are excluded from standard hydroforming operations. Can Hydroforming Replace All Sheet Metal Forming Processes? No, hydroforming is not suitable for all geometries or cost-sensitive high-volume production environments. Conventional stamping remains more economical for simpler parts at scale because tooling costs are lower and cycle times are faster. Hydroforming requires sealed die systems, high-pressure fluid management, and longer cycle times that increase per-part cost relative to stamping in large production runs. Simple flat or single-curvature parts offer no geometric advantage from hydroforming and are produced more efficiently through conventional sheet metal processes. Re-entrant geometries and open-profile shapes that cannot be enclosed in a die cavity are outside the scope of hydroforming entirely. The process complements rather than replaces conventional forming methods, addressing the specific subset of applications where geometric complexity and part consolidation justify the higher process cost for Sheet Metal . Begallie 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data.
